subtopic: MR. CHURCHILL    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS"

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. CHURCHILL    REFERENCE TO EDITORIAL IN WINNIPEG "FREE PRESS"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege relating to an editorial which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press dated Monday, April 4, 1960.
The editorial, in part, reads as follows:
The most serious offence that a Canadian cabinet minister can commit is to misinform the House of Commons on a factual matter of public business. Of this offence Mr. Churchill, Minister of Trade and Commerce, has recently been guilty three times over. The true information about Canada's present position in the field of trade and foreign debt, together with Mr. Churchill's large package of misinformation, are shown today in an adjoining column.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I quote another paragraph in the same editorial, which is as follows:
Having distorted the figures, Mr. Churchill used them to show that Canada has no need to worry about the prospects of its foreign trade or its accelerating plunge into foreign debt. The government's foreign economic policy, in short, is based on Mr. Churchill's optimistic analysis which, in turn, is based on false figures.
Then I quote a third paragraph from the same editorial:
Meanwhile, by distorting the known official facts and misleading parliament, the government and the nation, Mr. Churchill has discredited himself as a reliable witness on the vital questions of policy.
Mr. Speaker, every one of those three paragraphs is false. The figures that I used in the speech I made in the House of Commons on March 21 and March 22 were derived from official dominion bureau of statistics publications. No figures were distorted; the known official facts were not distorted; no figures were false or erroneous.
The same false statement about using wrong figures occurs in the heading of an article on the same page of the Winnipeg Free Press written by one who designates himself by the initials B.H. The heading is, "Wrong Conclusion from Wrong Figure". The article by B.H. on which the editorial writer purports to base his editorial is similarly misleading and false.
Mr. Speaker, I did not misinform or mislead the House of Commons either deliberately or otherwise. There are other things I might say; there is more detail into which I might go, but I think I have said enough to indicate what is in my mind regarding this matter.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement concerning world refugee year. Today has been designated as a day on which special efforts will be made in countries around the world to focus public attention on the world refugee problem in order to encourage increased contributions from the public to the world refugee year program.
In Canada a unique program has been planned by the appropriate private agencies. As far as I am aware no other country is attempting anything like it. Mayors and reeves of municipalities across Canada will be proclaiming the last week of April to be national austerity week. During that week Canadians will be requested to deny themselves some luxury or pleasure on which they would ordinarily spend money and to send the money so saved to their local world refugee year committee. In the course of this special week, tag days and other methods of fund raising will be employed in aid of world refugee year.
The government has agreed to follow up the interest engendered by national austerity week by authorizing post offices across the country to use a special world refugee year postal cancellation during May and June. It is hoped that this special postal cancellation, which will read "World Refugee Year-Remember and Give", will remind Canadians during the final months of world refugee year to make their contribution to their local world refugee year committee.
Hon. members will recall that in early March I announced that the government would be prepared to extend the program for the admission of tuberculous refugees and

Inquiries of the Ministry their families to Canada if suitable arrangements could be worked out with the provincial governments which administer the sanatoria. It may be appropriate for me to state at this time that the replies received from a number of provincial governments have been encouraging, and we have therefore begun the preliminary selection and processing of additional tuberculous cases in the refugee camps. Until these processes have been completed it is, as I said yesterday, not possible to give the specific number of tuberculous refugees and their dependents who may ultimately be admitted to Canada for rehabilitation.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN PROGRAM
speechtext:
I am sure all members of this house will join with the minister in impressing upon the Canadian people the desirability of their making a contribution toward a solution of this problem. The government does not, however, in the statements which have been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, indicate its intention to extend its own contribution. It is true that the minister has announced that more tubercular cases will be processed, but I suspect this is largely due to the underestimate which was made of the total number of tubercular refugees who could be covered by the original grant appropriated for that purpose by the government.
In any event, the minister does not indicate if the government has accepted the representations made by the national welfare council and other voluntary social and religious organizations which asked for assistance so they in turn might make some definite contribution toward the alleviation of the refugee problem. The criticism, of course, also has prevailed that Canada has been prepared only to take those tubercular cases that were capable of rehabilitation, that the hard core which remains a very substantial part of the tubercular refugee problem, was not one to which Canada was giving the kind of support it should.
It may be that the minister will take note of these observations and find ways and means of integrating them in the program on which Canada has officially embarked. The solution of the refugee problem is something that commends itself to the conscience of all civilized people. It is appropriate that Canada, a country with excellent tubercular treatment institutions, should in this way join with other countries in trying to resolve this world refugee problem.
I venture to express the hope in taking my seat that the government likewise will be continually interested in the resolution of another refugee problem, that in Palestine.

These are problems that require the careful attention of civilized peoples whose governments are called upon to make a contribution to the solution of these very vital humanitarian problems.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING CANADIAN PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this group has always expressed concern for the welfare of people who are suffering anywhere. On that account we are pleased to hear the minister's announcement which indicates that Canadians will make some personal contributions and sacrifices in support of action by the federal and provincial governments.
In view of this response on the part of various organizations and individuals to do more in connection with making world refugee year a success I urge the government to give further leadership by increasing the number who can be assisted as the result of government action, through responding favourably to representations made to it by such organizations as the Canadian welfare council and religious and other bodies across Canada.

speechtext: Speaking on the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. Perhaps the time has come when this house should examine the practice it is getting into with respect to the asking of supplementary questions. I regret that I do not have in front of me the actual references. However, I have been concerned about this matter because, while Your Honour has allowed-and as I recall it all your predecessors have done so or have been inclined to do so-reasonable latitude with respect to the asking of supplementary questions, I suggest that during this session particularly the supplementary questions, which previously have been confined to probably not more than one or at the most two on any one subject, have been extended on a number of occasions so that as many as six or more supplementary questions have been asked on one subject. And as somebody behind me says, "and of cross-examination". It is clearly such an enlargement of the principle with respect to the asking of questions as to be out of order. When we had a discussion on a point of order not so long ago, and when I raised a point of order with regard to questions, we were told that this was the custom and it was suggested that I was seeking to limit, or to ask Your Honour to limit, the rights of the opposition with respect to the asking of questions and to run counter to custom.
At that time I pointed out that what I was concerned about was a trend developing which, if not called in question, would then be regarded as having become customary. It is for that particular reason that I now

raise this point of order with regard to supplementary questions. If we as a House of Commons do not examine the practice that we are beginning to follow, I am afraid we shall later be told that because the matter was not raised, this has become a custom.
The particular ruling I have in mind is one by Mr. Speaker Glen no longer ago than 1943, in which Mr. Speaker Glen said this. I am not quoting his words verbatim, but I know I reflect their sense accurately. He said that supplementary questions are not allowed by our rules. That was as recently as 1943. There have been rulings by speakers since that time which perhaps were not quite as strict as that by Mr. Speaker Glen but which certainly restricted the asking of supplementary questions to not more than one or two on any one point. Certaintly no hon. member, as I recall it in looking at this ruling, has the absolute right to ask a supplementary question.
I submit in brief that the rules of this house, as interpreted by the Speaker of the House, make it clear that supplementary questions are not allowed by right and that if allowed they are allowed occasionally only as a matter of latitude, usually only in order to clear up what would otherwise be some misunderstanding or some gap in the information that had been given in the original answer.
I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that we are falling into the practice not of raising supplementary questions for that purpose but of using them for the purpose of engaging in debate at a time when debate is not supposed to be taking place. Debate is supposed to take place only when we reach the matters which are on the order paper for discussion as part of the regular business of the house.
I would be prepared to discuss the matter at greater length if Your Honour desires me to do so, but I raise the matter now because, in view of what was said by the hon. member for Assiniboia, I think if the matter is not raised at this time we shall be told later, if we raise it, that the practice has become a custom and should be allowed. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is wrong to allow it to become a custom because it is contrary to the rules of this house.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. McGrath (St. John's East):
maintopic: I960 THE BUDGET ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock last evening I was leading into the subject of the United States defence bases in Newfoundland and Labrador which were granted to the United States government by the imperial government at the outset of the second world war in 1940. I referred to the fact that although these bases had been leased for a period of 99 years without the advice or consent of the people of Newfoundland at that time, no protection whatsoever had been provided for the pension rights of the people who were employed on those bases.
I referred yesterday to the fact that this is a matter of concern to other hon. members of this house who have these bases located in their constituencies. I have in mind St. John's West, where a United States naval base is located at Argentia; Grand Falls-White Bay-Ladrabor, where the United States air force has a location at Goose Bay, and Humber-St. George's where the United States has the Ernest Harmon air force base situated on the west coast of Newfoundland at Stephenville around which a town of some 8,000 people has grown.
This is a very important question, because I think the time has come when this whole situation should be carefully studied and reappraised in connection with the future disposition of these bases. I am founding this contention on the fact that only a few weeks ago the United States government and our own Department of National Defence announced that Pepperrell air force base at St. John's would terminate its operations by September 1 of this year. This news was not unexpected, because warnings had gone out several years ago. Yet in spite of the fact that representations have been made by the employees over the past ten years or more, it was only upon realization that a close-down was imminent that the right of these people to a pension was recognized.
I mentioned earlier that I was happy to refer to this subject because our relations with the United States military forces in Newfoundland during the past 20 years have been,
The Budget-Mr. McGrath
I suggest, without parallel anywhere in the world. Our relations with United States service personnel have been exemplary. Many thousands of our people have found constant employment with them. These men and women from the United States are fully integrated into our society and communities. They take an active part in community affairs and in sporting events, and they have generally been good neighbours. They will be very greatly missed. I should like on this occasion, on behalf of my constituents, to acknowledge publicly our deep sense of appreciation and our deep sense of loss with regard to the departure of these good friends.
Now, however, the question arises as to the future disposition of these bases. For example, Pepperrell air force base, which was founded in 1941, originally as a military establishment and subsequently as an air force base, contributes at the present time approximately $12 million annually to the economy of St. John's. Hon. members will realize without difficulty that the loss of this sum annually to a city of less than 100,000 people is substantial and constitutes a severe economic blow. This is accounted for mainly by the fact that there are approximately 5,000 air force personnel employing some 1,200 civilians. The civilian payroll alone reaches a total of $4,576,000 annually. The annual rate of pay per week for Canadian citizens employed on this installation is $81.
As I said, this base was established on a 99-year lease which means, in effect, that it was not similar in all respects to military camps as we have come to know them in Canada. These buildings are permanent buildings. The total value of the properties located at Pepperrell, near St. John's, exceeds $40 million. These include a fully independent, self-contained hospital; magnificent school buildings, beautiful large living quarters of brick construction, as well as all the other buildings that go toward making up a large military establishment.
The St. John's Evening Telegram in its issue of January 12, 1960 said:
A "deactivated" Pepperrell air force base-a technically-abandoned base on Canadian territory, which was not Canadian when the territory was handed over and which was granted more as a gift than as part of a business contract and without prior consultation with its original owners, seems to have the makings of a very interesting international question.
In the same issue, with reference to the properties on Pepperrell air base, the Telegram said:
In any event, what is to happen to the magnificent, multimillion dollar plant located on the base in the

The Budget-Mr. McGrath
shape of a splendid hospital, a fine school, family homes and barracks, that, without too much difficulty, could be turned into apartments.
Are they to be left to deteriorate, as they inevitably must, when Newfoundland is short of classrooms, hospital beds, housing accommodation? Surely there must be some way, some arrangement that could be made to put such costly and worthwhile buildings and other facilities to work to fill a great need.
It is true that we are desperately in need of hospital beds, and that there is a magnificent hospital located on this establishment. We have been pressing for an armoury at St. John's, and there is a magnificent armoury at the Pepperrell air force base in addition to classrooms and buildings of all descriptions.
Probably what is more important is the fact that with the withdrawal of the United States air force a vacuum will be created in the North American defence structure. No one is prepared to concede that the day of so-called conventional war is a thing of the past. On the contrary, the future existence of civilization depends on hostilities being restricted to such small conventional wars. I raise this point to emphasize to my colleagues in the government and particularly to the Minister of National Defence the need of consultation on the part of his department with the joint chiefs of staff of the Canadian services, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Defence Production in respect to this question.
I will be the first to concede that the allocation of the defence budget across Canada is made not on a per capita, regional or proportional basis but purely on the basis of strategic need. Newfoundland is the Gibraltar of Canada, of North America. It is Canada's easternmost frontier. It has only a token force of Canadian military personnel. With the withdrawal of the United States air force, and with the question being raised as to the future disposition of the facilities at Pepperrell, now is the time when we should give consideration to providing a military establishment there on Canada's easternmost frontier comprising members of the Canadian army, navy or R.C.A.F. as the case may be. There is a need for such a Canadian establishment at the Gibraltar of North America, which has always been fortified, if for no other reason than to provide a token force, to establish and maintain sovereign rights and to recognize the strategic location of this part of the country.
As I have said, we have a ready-made military installation in Canada in which since


1940 Canada and the people of Newfoundland have had no say. What is to be its future? We know that Pepperrell is to be vacated, but what will be the future of the United States air force base at Stephenville? It is primarily a fighter base. We know from discussions in the house that the trend in the general defence policy of North America adopted by Canada and the United States is away from the fighter to the ballistic missile and other weapons. There seems to be no justification for this installation, which is primarily a fighter base, basing interceptor squadrons. What is to happen to the town of 8,000 people that has been built up in that area over the past ten years should the installation follow the course at Pepperrell and terminate its operations?
These questions require careful and serious study on the part of our government in consultation with the government of the United States through its department of state and department of defence. This is a domestic question certainly falling within the province of the federal government. It points to a need to reappraise the situation on the east coast with regard to our own military installations.
The Royal Canadian Navy has great strength in Nova Scotia, which is the traditional home of the navy in Canada and will always be so. Surely there is a requirement for larger air force establishment at St. John's to fill the vacuum created by the withdrawal of United States troops. I suggest that without undue delay this question be given serious thought by the government of Canada, and that consultation be initiated with the United States government relating to the eventual disposition of United States properties in Canada.
I should like at this time with the consent of the house to have printed as an appendix to Hansard a description of the physical buildings and properties at Pepperrell air force base, so that hon. members may see more clearly exactly what I am talking about. May I have the consent of the house for this purpose?

speechtext:
I thank the house for this courtesy, Mr. Speaker. Before I leave the subject may I at this time publicly acknowledge the understanding, co-operation, kindness and consideration shown by his excellency the ambassador of the United States and members of his staff and the United States air force authorities in Ottawa during the weeks this question has been under discussion. It is as a result of their endeavours and the endeavours of the consul general of the United States in St. John's, and the understanding of the United States air force authorities, that the people who are being laid off from some of these bases, particularly Pepperrell, are to be granted pension rights under the United States civil service retirement act.
Before I resume my seat I would like to refer briefly to one other subject which affects my constituency. I would like to refer to the surplus labour situation in the iron ore mines of Bell island. I draw the attention of the house to the fact that, notwithstanding what may have been said to the contrary by learned members of the opposition from Newfoundland, particularly the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the Minister of Labour wrote to the premier of Newfoundland on October 5, 1959 following his visit to Bell island to personally survey the situation there, where some 600 men were laid off last year as a result of the closing down of one of the three shafts of the mine. As a result of his personal appraisal of the situation he recommended to the premier of Newfoundland that they, that is, the federal and provincial governments, share in a vocational training scheme in order to enable particularly the younger people on Bell island 79951-0-190
The Budget-Mr. McGrath -where there are, I might add, over 14,000 people wholly dependent on one industry-to get some vocational training to provide greater scope and opportunity for them, and for men of middle age who know nothing but work in the mines over the past years. This need has been recognized by the people of Bell island, including members of the labour movement and civil leaders. It is a very serious problem. The need to relocate those people in other sections of the country or of the province, as the case may be, where jobs are more readily available and where they could have greater scope because of newly acquired skills, is obvious.
I am sorry to say that although the minister's letter was acknowledged on October 8, 1959 and advice was given by the premier that the matter was being referred to his colleague, the provincial minister of labour, that is where the matter stands at the moment. I am raising this matter at this time, sir-

In any event, Mr. Speaker, if the question of the learned member for Essex East does warrant attention, surely if the government of Newfoundland with greater revenue than ever before cannot afford a

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau 50-50 arrangement with the federal government to provide vocational training for about 500 people, then I suggest it does not deserve to carry on the government.
My purpose in raising this particular question at this time is to impress upon my learned colleagues in the opposition, particularly my good friend for Bonavista-Twillingate, who is not here-maybe the hon. member for Essex East will convey this to him-the necessity of his interceding with his good friend and mentor the premier of Newfoundland, on behalf of my constituents on Bell island. Please ask him whether he will at least look into the possibility of acceding to the request of the Minister of Labour in providing that badly needed vocational training for those displaced miners on Bell island.
In closing, I thank the house for its indulgence in listening to my remarks, which I have tried to make of a national character rather than purely local in scope because, as I said, the question of the United States bases affects not only my constituency but other ridings in the country. The question of the surplus labour situation on Bell island is one which concerns all of us in Newfoundland. I would hope that we can forget our partisanship long enough to resolve some of these problems, particularly as they apply to our people. After all, they are not interested in the colour of our political flag when their stomachs are empty. I would ask, sir, that these questions be treated in the way that the United States bases question has been.
I might add, sir, that I like to feel-and I am sure the hon. member for Humber-St. George's (Mr. Batten) would agree with me -that it is because of the fact that those problems have been kept out of the public forum and have not been made partisan political questions that the solution has been a satisfactory one, particularly in regard to pensions. I would hope that the same spirit would guide us in discussion with regard to the future of the displaced miners of Bell island and other questions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Monday, when the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) rose to comment on the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), I was preparing to listen closely to him in view of our friendly


relations and also because of the fact that he represents the constituency next to mine in Montreal.
I was quite disappointed however, because if you analyse his speech and leave out the quotations, there is just nothing left.
He gave us a definition of the word "create". To create, he says, is to do something out of nothing. On the basis of that definition, there is little to be done with his speech, because there was nothing in it.
He managed to say, after the minister's budget speech, that we have a great, an outstanding Minister of Finance.
That reminded me of the speeches we used to hear regularly in Quebec from Union Nationale members, about a certain politician they described as being the greatest since confederation.
While we are on the subject, may I remind some of the Quebec Conservative backbenchers that this is not the Quebec legislature, where duplessism is the keyword; this is the House of Commons of Canada, where there are standing orders which are applied with fairness and justice.
A number of Conservative backbenchers from Quebec use this house as a sounding-board to extol the merits of a man of whom, unfortunately, they are disciples.
Mr. Duplessis, as the dictator of Quebec for many years, caused untold harm to Quebec and to Canadians on the national level. We were misjudged because of the stand he took and because of his insubordinate and reactionary turn of mind. It is not surprising that from time to time we hear remarks such as those made last Friday by the member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). However, in view of the position he holds, I think that before making his speech he should have sought information about the true feelings of the right-minded majority of French Canadians.
It has never entered the minds of Quebec people and French Canadians to impose their views on the other provinces. But I understand that Mr. Duplessis' attitudes led many of our fellow citizens outside the province of Quebec to believe that we objected to everything coming from Ottawa or from the other provinces. He always gave the impression that Quebec refused to compromise. But this was only the opinion of one man and of a few of his followers who, unfortunately, were entrusted with the future of the province.

When you know the French Canadians well, you realize they want to live their lives fully as Canadians, within the framework of the Canadian confederation, sharing the rights and responsibilities of all Canadian provinces.
This is something you personally understand, Mr. Speaker, and I commend you for the attitude you show publicly towards Canadians, not only since your appointment as Speaker, but always.
The Speaker of this house deserves the admiration and respect of all Canadians, and most particularly of French Canadians, whom he sincerely understands and admires.
But I would ask my French Canadian fellow citizens, who are sitting in this house under the Tory label, to stop behaving as henchmen of Maurice Duplessis and the Union Nationale. They should at last understand that, as they have been sitting here for three years, they are here to deal with national matters, on a national level and in a purely national spirit.
That should not prevent them from expressing, from time to time the views of the province they represent here, but they should in doing so, remain conscious of the fact that we are living in a Canadian confederation which extends from coast to coast.
The prime objective of federal members should be the greatness of their country, of all their country, and the welfare of Canadians, of all Canadians. The leader of the government here is not the leader of the Quebec government, but the leader of the Canadian government. My Conservative colleagues from Quebec seem to forget it sometimes.
This is so true that when the member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin), addressing a Manitoba audience, stated, as reported in the press, that Mr. Duplessis had been obsessed by autonomy, none other than the great treasurer who controls the sinews of war for the Union Nationale, saw fit to denounce him to the whole province, right in the legislature, and to call him a child.
After the remarks made by the Hon. Gerard Martineau, the member for Mont-magny-L'Islet felt bound to go back on his opinion and to explain himself, in order to reingratiate himself, not with the leader of the Canadian government, but with the big chief of the Union Nationale.
Such a situation is unbearable for a member of the Canadian parliament.
79951-0-190i
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
In saying this, I do not want to point personally to the hon. member for Laval because, as far as I know, he himself never walked into that trap. But, as I mentioned earlier, his statement that the Minister of Finance is a great Minister of Finance reminds me that the front and backbenchers of the Union Nationale, in my province, were always saying that Mr. Duplessis was the greatest premier since confederation.
Mr. Maurice Duplessis is now dead. God has judged him and history will judge him. When the hon. Mr. Sauve replaced him, a new mood spread over the province of Quebec. Already the Union Nationale and the Conservative members had started to say that he too was the greatest premier we ever had in the province of Quebec. Since both of them were the greatest premiers, I wonder where this leaves the present premier of Quebec.
To come back to the Minister of Finance, as I have just said, the member for Laval exclaimed, in his charming candour, that he was a great, great, great Minister of Finance.
When he sings the praises of the Minister of Finance, of the Prime Minister, and of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, he reminds me a little of a purring cat waiting to be patted.
Well, after the few remarks he made, he had his pat, his reward, when the Minister of Finance turned towards him and gave him a big smile. There are less of those purring cats nowadays, that used to keep close to cabinet members looking for a smile, a pat or something else. But we notice this year, since the appointment of parliamentary secretaries, that many of the purring cats keep huddled in their corners and are no longer heard from.
After hearing and studying the budget speech and after surveying the reactions of various groups of businessmen across the country, I can only say that this year's budget is much smaller than Conservative members, through the hon. member for Laval, would have us think, and that the Minister of Finance is not that great.
Of course, since confederation, it did not happen very often that a Conservative government, through its Minister of Finance, could in a budget speech forecast a slight surplus, and I understand the quite childish satisfaction felt by the Minister of Finance

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau when he introduced his budget, and by the government members and later on by Conservative backbenchers.
I must say frankly that, as a Canadian citizen, I am happy that the budget could finally be somewhat balanced and I wholeheartedly hope that the minister's forecast will prove to be right, although I doubt it very much.
But I cannot forget that, if this year the minister was able to forecast a surplus of $12 million for next year, it is because of the tax increases of last year, which yield approximately half a billion dollars each year to the treasury.
Nor can I forget the 800,000 unemployed in our country, about whom the Minister of Finance did not seem to care very much.
I cannot, forget either the 100,000 civil servants whom the Minister of Finance did not take into account in the salary increases.
I cannot forget either the businessmen and industrialists across the country, who suffer and many of whom are facing bankruptcy because of the credit restrictions laid down by the Bank of Canada in collusion with the Minister of Finance.
And the Conservative backbenchers ignore those issues which are vital for all Canadians, and hang on to what seems to them a safety belt after those discouraging and depressing deficits of the last three years.
According to those Conservative backbenchers, Mr. Speaker, all is for the best in the best of worlds. In their view there is no unemployment. They see no credit restrictions, and they think that civil servants are satisfied. Like children, they are wild with joy. They are happy. Therefore civil servants must be happy too, as must be businessmen, leaders of industry, and even the unemployed.
Like them, we should follow in the footsteps of the hon. member for Laval who declares that the Minister of Finance is a great, great, great minister.
But, Mr. Speaker, even if, as a Canadian, I expressed some hope because of the $12 million surplus announced by the Minister of Finance, I say again that, because of our past experience, I cannot share their views and call the present holder of the finance portfolio a great minister.
Since the Conservative party took over in 1957, the government and the Minister of Finance have increased this country's national


debt by more than a billion dollars, thus increasing the servicing of the debt by several hundred million dollars a year.
For the year just ended, the Minister of Finance, a few days before his budget speech, confirmed to us that the deficit exceeded $400 million. Is that something about which Canadians may rejoice? The only happy ones are the Conservative backbenchers.
During the years 1945-57, the government under a Liberal prime minister succeeded in lowering the national debt by $2,413,000,000, which reduced the servicing of the debt accordingly. In less than three years, the Conservative government has again increased the national debt by more than a billion dollars, thus adding some $500 million yearly to the servicing of the debt.
Mr. Speaker, I do not hesitate to state in this house, and before the whole nation, that in less than three years, this government and the Minister of Finance have destroyed the results of 11 years of good and sound Liberal administration.
However, Conservative backbenchers are rejoicing and are satisfied with the mirage summoned before their eyes. I did not know they were naive enough to be satisfied with so little.
The hon. member for Laval told us in this house last Monday, that if he were sitting in the opposition, he would be so discouraged by the finance minister's budget speech for this year that he would resign.
That shows very little knowledge of the Leader of the Opposition and of members who are sitting by his side. Like our leader, our sole purpose is the greatness of our country and the welfare of our fellow citizens.
What we have done since we have been in the opposition has been merely to ask the government to give a sound administration to this country and to ensure the welfare of Canadians.
Discouraged? We could have been that long before today, when we saw our country so badly administered by this government. But we are not discouraged. We never are, and never will be. We shall not let up. Quite the contrary, we shall keep on working towards the goal I have just indicated.
We have a role to play in this house, and neither the member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages), nor his Conservative backbencher friends, will prevent us from playing it.

However, we are astounded by the naivete of Conservative members who content themselves with so little. In view of their puerile attitude, we are determined to fight on for our Canadian fellow citizens, confident that we represent the views of the great majority of Canadians who are only waiting for the opportunity of sweeping out of office a government that is showing arrogance, inconsistency, complacency, and which is leading us, without any doubt, to economic chaos and to unemployment.
The people are not happy. The unemployed are not happy. Businessmen are not happy. Industrialists are not happy.

speechtext: Neither are the Liberals.

maintopic: I960 THE BUDGET ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Only those dear Conservative backbenchers are happy.

maintopic: I960 THE BUDGET ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Liberals are not.

maintopic: I960 THE BUDGET ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why don't you do something about the unemployment in your constituency?
We wonder why the member for Laval, who, epitomizing the thought of his backbencher friends, stated, I don't know on what basis, that civil servants were happy with the $15 million granted to a third of them. I am glad for those civil servants who will get a small salary increase, and I take this opportunity to point out to the Minister of Finance that it would now be proper to show our gratitude to those ladies who, in parliament, are our collaborators; I mean the members' secretaries. They are not only our stenographers, they are real collaborators. They show unlimited devotion and they have great responsibilities. They do not hesitate to stay on the job until late, to carry on the work they have undertaken, and what is more, they defend the member for whom they work. They deserve not only our admiration, but also all our gratitude. I hope that, as a token of our gratitude, the Minister of Finance will grant them the raise they deserve.
As to the 100,000 who have been ignored, I would strongly advise the hon. member for Laval and his colleagues to take note of the comments of various officials of civil service organizations, which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen for April 1, 1960. It is reported that the joint action committee of Canadian civil service organizations expressed bitter disappointment at the salary increases announced by the Minister of Finance
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau in his budget speech, which involved only a third of the civil servants. The report added that there was general dissatisfaction.
Mr. Ken Green, of the national defence employees association, stated that the commission had been ignored and that increases should have been extended to all civil servants. Mr. Fred Whitehouse, president of the Civil Service Federation of Canada, said with a touch of humour that civil servants would hit the ceiling. He added that the increase, which had been expected for all civil servants, applied only to one third of them.
Mr. Marshall, president of the professional institute, indicated that civil servants were not being given full satisfaction.
Those are only a few comments from officials of civil service groups. I am sure they adequately represent the feelings of all Canada's civil servants.
Tory backbenchers are happy, but civil servants are not, and they still remember the Minister of Finance's statement that even if funds were available, civil servants would not get the increases they have been demanding.
The unemployed are also dissatisfied. The 800,000 people who, across Canada, would like to earn a decent living but cannot, surely do not share the feelings expressed by the hon. member for Laval, and are quite disappointed that the Minister of Finance has mentioned nothing that might be of some help.
Proportionately, Canada has twice as many unemployed as the United States. That is an intolerable situation. Instead of rejoicing at the few crumbs they are getting from the Minister of Finance, Conservative backbenchers should give serious thought to the plight of family heads who are unable to find jobs and who, much to their sorrow, have to let their families live in want.
Being jobless, many of those family heads have lost their car and some furniture, because they could not meet the payments. Many have had to take their children out of schools and colleges because they were no longer able to pay for their education.
Instead of rejoicing, Conservative backbenchers should feel pity for those unfortunate people and insist time and time again that the government correct the situation once and for all, and not tolerate such a disastrous state of affairs affecting hundreds

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau of thousands of families in a country with unlimited natural resources and supposed to be rich.
If we were able to find the necessary funds for our war effort-and rightly so-it is inconceivable that in a country such as ours and in peacetime means cannot be devised to provide work for our bread winners and citizens.
The member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and several other opposition members made constructive suggestions to the government. But as the suggestions originated from the opposition, they were ignored just as the employment situation in this country is ignored. However, while the unemployed are unhappy and opposition members are anxious to see that crucial problem settled, Conservative backbenchers are happy.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, they are happy, but business, industry, the civil service and the jobless are quite unhappy about the government's attitude.
Had he been of any consequence, the member for Laval would have been the laughing stock of all textile plant owners when he said that they were satisfied with the budget and that all their troubles were over.
Nevertheless, a statement by Mr. W. H. Young, vice president and general manager of the Hamilton Cotton Co. Ltd. is to be found in the Hamilton Spectator of April 1, 1960 to the effect that the budget had no significance for them, and another by Mr. E. D. James, vice president of Comos Imperial Mills Ltd., to the effect that the budget was most disappointing and the technical changes in the wording of tariff regulations would not in the least reduce costs to textile mills.
This year, construction, which has often been considered the basis of our economy, is experiencing a dangerous and even alarming decline. Businessmen and industrialists see their profits dwindle gradually. Credit restrictions are making it hard for them to stay in business.
The Prime Minister went to great pains to tell us in a television broadcast last fall that there was no tight money policy in this country.
The Minister of Finance repeated the same thing. Let us ask industrialists, businessmen, merchants or workers whether they can easily borrow at the bank the money they need to successfully operate their business. They know in advance the answer they will get

from the bank manager. They will be told that there is no money available for them at the present time.
The Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance may deny the government's responsibility for this state of affairs, but the facts prove that full responsibility for the tight money policy rests on the present government.
Indeed, what has happened, Mr. Speaker, since the Conservatives took office?
In order to fulfil a few of the many irresponsible promises they had made to the voters, they had to go to a terrible expense and plunge the federal administration into deficits that had never been equalled so far. To cover those deficits, the government had to resort to loans and particularly to the famous debt conversion operation.
As a result, whatever money was available in banks or elsewhere went to the government, which became the country's heaviest borrower. The government grabbed money which otherwise would have been available to small borrowers, thus causing interest rates to soar. This has forced every Canadian taxpayer to pay more for servicing the national debt which in two years has risen by one billion dollars, raising the interest payments by $249 million a year.
The increase in interest rates had an impact on the borrowing of school boards and municipalities. Those corporations, when they are able to secure loans at all, have to pay an interest rate often exceeding 7 per cent. And who ultimately pays the interest charges paid by municipalities and school boards? Who pays for the increase in servicing the national debt? The taxpayer, the small property owners whose assessments rise accordingly.
If the Tory government had administered things wisely, it would at least have balanced its budget since 1957; it would not have had to resort to enormous borrowing, and the borrowed money would still be available to others at a reasonable interest rate. We would not be facing today that tight money policy which is driving hundreds upon hundreds of people to the wall and contributing to unemployment.
The Prime Minister, just like the Minister to Finance, wants to deny the evidence, by maintaining that they have nothing to do with the decisions of the governor of the Bank of Canada. Those two ministers accused

the chartered banks of being responsible for the tight money policy. Nothing is farther from the truth. The decisions taken by the governor of the Bank of Canada are completely endorsed by the government. The Bank of Canada is under the jurisdiction of parliament and, more particularly, of the Minister of Finance.
If the governor of the Bank of Canada were to take some action and adopt attitudes contrary to the government's, he would have no other alternative but to tender his resignation. However, to my knowledge, neither the Minister of Finance, nor the Prime Minister, nor any member of this government has denounced the governor of the Bank of Canada with regard to tight money policy. I have not heard it said that the governor of the Bank of Canada had considered tendering his resignation to the Minister of Finance.
It therefore means that this government, in order to meet the dire results of its inexperience and its lack of responsibility endorses the Bank of Canada in its tight money policy.
The Minister of Finance would have the Canadian public believe that there is no tight money policy in this country. He had solemnly promised that, under a Conservative government, there would be no credit restrictions. That is just another promise broken by the Conservative government.
During the present session, I heard on various occasions the Minister of Finance, with a few Conservative backbenchers in his wake, exclaim that the leader of the government and the Conservatives had fulfilled all their promises.
I indict that statement as false, and so do our people. The leader of the Conservative party, who is now Prime Minister, and the Conservative government did not fulfil their promises.
Yet, if I refer to the Toronto Star of December 2, 1957, I find the following statement, which the Prime Minister is supposed to have made at a Conservative convention in Ottawa. Mr. Diefenbaker, is said to have stated at the time. "A promise given is a promise kept." And he added that 10 per cent of the promises he had made had been kept.
He suggested that a government which did not keep its promises was doomed to defeat.
I would like, this afternoon, to recall some of the promises made by the leader of the
The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
government during election campaigns, promises which have not yet been fulfilled, even after three years of administration. A whole litany of unfulfilled promises could be listed.
We had been promised a tax cut of $500 million a year. In the session which followed the coming into power of this Conservative government for the first time, taxes were reduced, because another election was in sight soon after. But right after the general election of 1958, instead of being reduced by $500 million, taxes were increased by the same amount. We had been promised a balanced budget. However, since the Conservative government has been in power, deficits have been as follows: 1958, $38,500, 000; 1959, $609,300,000;	1960, $405,800,000,
which makes a total of $1,053,700,000 in three years. Are these what we might call balanced budgets?
The Prime Minister had long been solemnly promising a bill of rights. Every year, since he has been in power, he introduces his bill, but never gives the house an opportunity either to consider it or to adopt it. There is another unfulfilled promise of the leader of the government.
When he was in the opposition, the Prime Minister kept promising to raise old age pensions to $60, but they are still at $55 a month.
The Prime Minister had promised new taxsharing arrangements between the federal government and the provinces. Apart from a few slight concessions made to the provinces, those arrangements have not yet been renewed; and that is another promise that has not been fulfilled by the Conservative government.
We had been promised that closure would be abolished in the House of Commons. Still another promise that has not been fulfilled by the Conservative party.
The province of Quebec had been promised the same representation in the cabinet which it used to have under the Liberal regime. That is another promise that had been made, but has not been kept.
We had been promised that Canadian National Railway employees would have their pensions increased. Another broken promise.
A Canadian coastal guard had been promised. We have no Canadian coastal guard yet. Another promise unfulfilled.
We had been promised that the special excise tax on cars would be abolished. Nothing has come out of that. Another promise that has not been fulfilled.
We had been promised a price support program for fish. Nothing has come out of that. Another promise that was not kept.

The Budget-Mr. Rouleau
We had been promised that the prairie farm rehabilitation act would apply everywhere in Canada. Another promise that has not been fulfilled.
We had been promised equal freight rates, to help agriculture and industry in the prairie provinces, so that they might compete with the rest of Canada. It has not been done. Another broken promise.
We had been promised that tuberculosis and mental illness would be included in the national hospital insurance plan. It has not been done. Another promise that has not been kept.
We had been promised a vigorous immigration policy. On the contrary, immigration is being slowed down. This is another promise on which the government has backed down.
We had been promised a reduction in unnecessary government expenditure. However, since the Conservatives have been in power, expenses have been rising steadily. Another unfulfilled promise.
