speechtext:
I hardly need mention that this is another unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised that immediate legislation would be introduced to provide for the control of water pollution. It has not been done. Another unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised that action would be taken for the greatest possible use to be made of the port of Churchill as an export centre for western grain. That has not been done; it is another unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised that Canadians would be encouraged, through fiscal measures, to invest their funds in such a way as to gain ownership of Canadian corporations. It has not been done, and it is a further unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised that a standard gauge railway would be substituted for the narrow gauge railway in Newfoundland. It has not been done, and it is still another unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised protection for manufacturing companies. Nothing has been done in that regard, and it is another unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised a change in the differential method used for taxing Canadian oil companies. It has not been done. There is another unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised a tax bill designed to help small industries, but that has not been done. Another unfulfilled promise.
We had been promised tax rebates for research into every field. It has not been done, and it is another unfulfilled promise.


That is only a partial list of the promises which the present government has left unfulfilled, and I wonder how Conservative backbenchers can be satisfied with such a government, just as I wonder how those who attended the Conservative convention in early December could cheer their leader when he stated that a promise made by a Conservative government was a promise kept. The Prime Minister, on that occasion, said that a government which backs down on its promises is doomed to defeat.
Mr. Speaker, after the list I have just given, I hardly need to say, what fate is in store for the present government.
According to a report published in La Presse for March 15 the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Balcer) stated in a speech delivered before the junior chamber of commerce of Montreal, that the difference between Canadian political parties is nothing more today than a difference between the teams that make up those parties. I refuse to accept that statement, because I think there are basic differences in the political outlook of the Liberal, Conservative and socialist parties. I feel sure, from the experience we have had in three years of Conservative administration, that the team which now leads the Liberal party is incomparably better and much more experienced than the Conservative team.
At the head of our party, we have a man of outstanding abilities. He has been a professor at the University of Toronto, and his ability has given him a reputation that will never be forgotten.
He raised Canada's reputation to unprecedented heights, and earned something which no Canadian had ever earned before: the Nobel peace prize.
He is the uncontested leader of the Liberal party. As Leader of the Opposition, his unquestionable skill is recognized by every member of this house, and by everyone who has had the privilege of following the debates in this house.
He is the future prime minister of Canada, and as such, he will give the country the sound administration we have a right to expect.
The Liberal party, in its 22 years of administration, and even through a terrible war, managed to provide a sound economy, to ensure a record prosperity and a high level of employment in Canada.
Three years of Conservative administration have resulted in heavy budget deficits and instability caused by a lack of administrative sense on the part of the leaders of the present government.

Canadians wanted to give the Conservatives another chance, but if we listen to the man in the street today, we realize that the people are longing for the day when they can replace the present government by a team that has always showed its mettle.
As I said at the outset, the member for Laval stated that if he were in the opposition, he would be so discouraged he would resign. I tell him again that, far from being discouraged, we are getting ready to restore to this country a sound administration and, until we appeal to the country, we will keep on doing in this house the work vested in us by the constitution.
As for the hon. member and the other Conservative backbenchers, they will not have to resign. The people of Canada will see at the next election that they are sent back home. The future of the country will be entrusted to other administrators.
That is what you were saying in 1958.

I do not want to question the sincerity of any one but, on the record of the last three years, we cannot have confidence in this government. Under the constitution, we still have two or three years to go before another election is held. I sincerely hope that the situation does not grow any worse.
This is a beautiful, great and wealthy country. To develop all the wealth with which it has been endowed, we need, at the head of the government, a team capable of developing our bountiful heritage. The Conservatives woefully failed at the task. It is up to us, to the press and the public in general, to prevent things from getting worse from now until the next election.
The natural resources of this country are unlimited. There is no reason why there should be any unemployment in Canada. No Canadian willing and able to work should suffer. We are still in a better position than the United States. We have a great part to play among the nations of the world.
What we have to do is to develop all our resources. Unfortunately, this government has been unable to do it. So, for the time being, we must make the best of the situation and prepare for the future.
In spite of what is going on at the present time, I have confidence in my country. I have confidence in my fellow citizens and I know that our own team is ready to watch over the destiny of Canada.
In a few years from now, we shall solve the problems that the present team cannot solve and we will continue to administer the affairs of our country so as to make it one of the great, one of the greatest and most peace-loving countries of the world.
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
(Text):

This is the fourth day of the debate on the budget, and I find myself puzzled and perplexed- and interested, of course-by one aspect of it, and that is that none of the five members of the previous government who sit in this house have yet taken part in the discussion. They do not ordinarily behave like non-combatants, and I have been asking myself just why there should have been this extraordinary unanimity of silence. What are they waiting for? New ammunition to come up from the base? Or do they expect that the newspapers will put down a barrage under which they can make an advance? If that should be their motive, I doubt whether they are going to find it a satisfactory one. At any rate, I suppose it will emerge soon.
One might imagine that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martini has been very busy with statistics-preparing his own ammunition, so flexible and so original-and one might imagine that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) is in company with his distinguished former chieftain whose life he is writing, and he will, no doubt, seek counsel there. But to come back to the newspapers. I doubt very much if any comfort will come to the opposition from that source. I shall read a short quotation from the Montreal Star which, so far as I recall, has not been very partial to our party over the years. This is what it has to say in part:
From the national point of view it is vital to pay our way, and that is what Mr. Fleming promises ... Indeed, a balanced budget in this year must be regarded as something in the nature of a minor miracle.
I like those words. And then the article goes on to say:
Its achievement reflects the integrity and growing stature of the Minister of Finance.
I like that, too, because it seems to me a plain statement of fact. I think the people of this country, even those who do not like us, are going to be impressed by the fact that we are now paying our way. I think as that sinks in it will be more and more impressive to them.
There is one quarter from which the opposition might have expected support. I refer to the Toronto Star. But I find the editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star the day after the budget somewhat perplexing. It is true the writer left some postern gates through which to return to the attack later on, but for the moment, it seems to me, he was pussy-footing.
The only interesting thing to me about the editorial was that it uses a word I have

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell never seen used before. It is a kind of highbrow word and I suppose one finds in use in the higher Liberal ranks. The editorial referred to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) as an "euphoric mariner". It is not an unpleasant word. I looked it up in the dictionary that we have in this chamber but it is not there. Apparently it is not the kind of word that hon. members of parliament use. It is perhaps over their heads.
It is not a parliamentary term.

It is not a term of insult. As a matter of fact "euphoria" is a rather interesting word. It is described as a word used to express well-being or the perfect ease and comfort of healthy persons. Now, who could have more feeling of well-being than the Minister of Finance at the present time?
It may be a false wellbeing, though.

It seems to me that the Star, perhaps unintentionally-it may be that they did not know the meaning of the word

 paid the minister a compliment. The word is not in the dictionary we have in the house and I do not suppose it would be in a Cambridge dictionary but it was in Murray's Oxford dictionary and that is what it means.
I repeat, I have no doubt that the Minister of Finance does feel a considerable amount of comfort. I would if I were in his position with a balanced budget. I think as one looks back one can see that it has not come about by accident but was based on long term planning and tenacity. After all, the Minister of Finance has had a long schooling in politics. He began in what is probably the most useful of all kinds of public service, as school trustee, went on to be an alderman and came down here as a member. We all know his record here. We are all aware of his zest for work. We all know he had a certain-what shall I say- aggressive quality which was very useful when he was in the opposition and which even now can be shown from time to time. He also had a considerable capacity for using the word "no" and that, I am sure, has been very useful in his present job.
Of course we must not forget that the minister has colleagues nor that he has the support of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) and his other colleagues, but when we look back and see that in those three years there has been a kind of steady relentless purpose moving toward a balanced budget we all must feel an admiration for the hon. gentlemen. He sought two years


ago to prepare for it. Last year he told us he hoped that this year it would come about, and here it is.
The Minister of Finance, of course, has his critics. As a matter of fact there was a period when he was subject to a great deal of very ignorant-I repeat, ignorant-criticism, some from people who should have known better and some from people who did not know at all and should not have undertaken to express opinions. I will admit there was a time when some people who should have known better where inclined to be critical. I believe that most of them have changed their minds and realized that the minister's long term planning was sound. I think they have realized that they were wrong.
Let us take, for example, the conversion loan. There were lots of people who talked foolishly about that, and I repeat, foolishly. What was the comment of people who knew about it at the time? I can remember very well what was said by a man whom I respect very much, a well-known businessman. I will never forget his words. He said, "What else could he have done?"
When you look at what happened in respect of that conversion loan and when you realize that in July of 1958 the average length of term of the outstanding victory bonds was 4.3 years and that by the first of September it was 13.3 years, anyone who understands debt and what it means will realize what a tremendous relief that was. I do not think any serious man in the world of finance will deny now that that operation was necessary and wise. They might say, "Oh well, he should have sold the bonds cheaper; he got too good a bargain from the public; he has probably made too good a sale," but that is not a very serious crime.
I do not think any serious person-and I must admit there are some people who are not serious who undertake to talk about it -will deny that that conversion loan was very wise indeed.
I would put in a caveat.

Well, caveats cost nothing. As I understand it you can put them in practically with no fee.
I also want to say a word about the premium on the Canadian dollar. I mentioned it especially because it is referred to in the amendment. The minister explained that at length in Toronto in January, I remember, and briefly again in the budget, and to me the answer to that is that so far as I am aware none of the people who have talked about it and wanted it wiped out is prepared to say how to do it. The minister has pointed out in his statements that without controls

and in a free market you cannot do it unless with fabulous expenditures. As I understand it, no one in the opposition has faced up to the question and said he is prepared to accept controls because no doubt he would find out quickly that if you are going to have financial controls as there were during the war time there will be other controls, too, and people are not in favour of them.
I believe every reasonable man will echo the words of the Montreal Star to which I have already referred that the balancing of the budget is the primary consideration, and when you tell them the budget is balanced they metaphorically sit back and say, "Thank God; that is a good thing." Let me read again the last sentence of the Montreal Star editorial:
-a balanced budget in. this year must be regarded as something in the nature of a minor miracle. This achievement reflects the integrity and growing stature of the Minister of Finance.
Surely those are words which the Minister of Finance can regard with deep satisfaction and pride.
So far I have been dealing with our own affairs which I believe the judgment of this country will pronounce good. I think even the bitterest opposition critic knows in his heart they are good. We had a list from the hon. member who spoke last of all kinds of things he alleged have not been done but for the most part they were small stuff. The judgment of the country will rely on the over-all fact that this minister has steered us into smoother seas by balancing the budget which was what everybody wanted.
If we lived in a world where everyone was in that position how happy we would be but we do not live in that kind of world. It is impressed on us more every day that we live in a shrinking world. We are living on each other's doorsteps with planes that go nearly a thousand miles an hour and with radio that goes instantaneously and tells other people in the world how we are all living. We are conscious of the fact that there are many countries-100 altogether, according to Paul Hoffman one time head of the Marshall plan- where poverty, ill health and despair prevail. Mr. Paul Hoffman was I suppose par excellence the man most skilled in international finance in providing relief to underdeveloped countries. He recognizes that there are 100 tragically poor countries, not including China, and that their population is 1,250 million.
Two thirds of the people of the world.

Yes, two thirds of the world's population. He speaks of the powerful
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell moral, political and business reasons for this. I underline the word "business". I believe myself that all of these three considerations represent, I was going to say the $64 question, but I would like to multiply it and say $128 question. Barbara Ward, the amazing woman who was once an editor of The Economist speaks of several break-throughs in these last ten years. Among others, she speaks of the break-through of those hungering for economic growth, hundreds of millions of them, and says that this and other break-throughs will expand explosively-I repeat, explosively -to make the sixties a period of challenge and change unequalled in human history. I wish I had the eloquence of a Lincoln or a Churchill, because I believe this is the thing which every one of us should take to heart. We know that in the back of our minds there are forebodings about the world we live in. We really get to the stage where we just try to forget them. But there they are.
I am going to read a few of the comments of world leaders which will underline the situation and give us the picture. First of all, I want to read wise words of our own Prime Minister. He speaks about the economic assistance to underdeveloped countries as a major and mandatory need if freedom is to be preserved in the world. Major and mandatory; that means something has to be done if freedom is to be preserved in the world.
What was the date of that reference?

I am not sure of the date. It is from a speech of the Prime Minister. I would' have to give the date to the hon. member later.
I want to read briefly from three or four other world opinions. First of all, a word from President Eisenhower on this question. When speaking of the crisis he said:
We face what could be a turning point in history, and we must act decisively.
Macmillan speaks of improving the conditions of life in the less developed countries of the world. He says it is one of the great challenges of our time. Then, this quotation from de Gaulle, which interested me more than any because it was not the kind of thing I would expect from him. He says this:
It is the duty of those who are best endowed and strongest to help others-those who are in want, those who are underprivileged. This, they must do if they themselves do not want to perish.
I repeat that. "If they themselves do not want to perish." There is a hard-boiled world leader, if you like, and this is what he has to say about the situation. I do not think any of us should take it lightly.
3G08

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
I have read these quotations because I want to make clear that those practical men are agreeing with Hoffman. I shall quote later from Eugene Black of the world bank, another businessman who has put this forward as tremendously important.
The results are rather disappointing. Hoffman said that: The result in 1950 was very disappointing. The per capita income in 1950 in underdeveloped countries is estimated at $110. In 1959 it should reach $125-$130. That is only $15-$20 in 10 years. The income has gone from approximately $110 to $125-$130. In other words, there has been an increase of only $15 to $20 in 10 years. Hoffman adds that this is dangerously slow. The average increase in the western nations between 1950 and 1957 was $300 per capita. In the United States it was $530. The rich are getting richer and the poor desperately poorer. Hoffman again says that the goal for 1969 should be $160.
When you look back at what was done in England and in western Europe you can see that there was a tremendous success achieved. The recipient nations were well organized. Hon. members recall how they were able to take the money and use it. Hon. members recall the loans we made to Britain in 1946. This is one of the first things we remember in parliament, the Minister of Finance, and I, who were new members at that time. As I recall, our loan was $1,250 million and the United States $3,750 million. They did a good job. As we remember, the Marshall plan worked almost a miracle under the management of that great man Hoffman. I just want to read a sentence from what Marshall said in 1947 at Harvard University:
Our policy is directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation, and chaos. Its purpose should be the revival of a working economy in the world so as to permit the emergence of political and social conditions in which free institutions can exist.
I commend these words to the intelligence of every one of us. I have quoted Hoffman's aim for 1970.
We are spending billions on defence. Speaking for myself, I do not see how we can let down our guard.

Just for my own
satisfaction will the hon. gentleman give me the date of his reference to Hoffman?

The quotation was taken from a speech Hoffman made in Toronto on October 19. I will send the hon. member a copy.
We are spending those billions in the hope -sometimes we find it a faint hope-that the equipment will never be used. We hope it will be a deterrent, but we can never be sure. We remember the old phrase, "Hope


deferred maketh the heart sick". I suppose what happens is that we try to tuck this into the back of our minds and not think about it. We watch new weapons being manufactured becoming obsolete before they are even ready for use. We see hundreds of millions of dollars spent for weapons which, as I say, are already obsolete. Meanwhile, another deterrent is not being adequately used. I refer to the deterrent of a revival of a working economy in the world, as Marshall said, so as to permit the emergence of political and social conditions in which free institutions can exist.
I think the feeling throughout the world is that war is not the only great enemy, but that poverty is another. There is no mystery as to how to aid countries. We learned how to do that from past failures. Money has been wasted but a great deal has been learned. The Hoffman organization under the United Nations makes searching inquiries before moneys are supplied. They survey natural resources and they give technical assistance. Recently there has been established a United Nations special fund, to which we have made a contribution, which will supply limited funds for capital development.
Let me read from Hoffman's pamphlet, entitled "One Hundred Countries" and his proposal at page 45. I wish to read also a short extract showing the almost miraculous results which can come about if the situation of these people can be improved ever so little. Here is what Hoffman says:
My proposal is this: That we-all of us together-* fix it as our goal to double in the 1960's, as compared with the 1950's, the annual per capita rate of economic growth in 100 countries and territories containing a billion and a quarter of the world's people. If we achieve this goal it will mean increasing the per capita economic growth rate of the less developed countries from an average of 1 per cent a year in the 1950's to an average of 2 per cent in the 1960's. To do this it will be necessary for the less developed countries to sustain an annual rate of economic growth of 4 per cent. This will mean a total increase of about 40 per cent and a per capita increase of nearly 25 per cent in 10 years. It will mean increasing per capita income from the estimated present figure of around $100 to around $125 in 1970. This means increasing per capita income in the 1960's by about 25 per cent per person or an average of about $2.50 per person per year.
I have one more quotation, and it will be my last quotation of any length. It struck me as so almost unbelievable that I want to read it. Hoffman said:
If the less developed countries receive additional foreign capital and increase local savings sufficient to lift their per capita incomes by only 1 per cent more a year over the coming decade, they might well offer to the United States alone a market for an estimated $14 billion of its exports in 1970. This would represent an increase of more than 100 per cent over total U.S. exports to the same areas

in 1958. And over the 10-year period, the total exports of all the developed countries to those areas. . . might be as much as $320 billion. In the long view, these 100 underdeveloped countries are for the United States and for the developed nations generally a great new economic frontier.
There you have the business side of it. We do not need to regard it as charity. There is a business side of it too. For instance, let us apply this to India. I was present in Montreal two years ago when the Minister of Finance presided over the commonwealth meeting there. So far as India is concerned, we can remind ourselves that in addition to being a member of the commonwealth India has a settled government, it has law and order and it has a well trained civil service. Therefore we can be reasonably certain that money applied there would be well spent.
I should like to read a sentence from a speech by Black of the world bank because I feel ever so strongly that this is a matter in which we should all be deeply concerned in our own self-interest. Black in speaking at Oxford a month ago dealt with the need of backward countries to develop efficiency and emphasized particularly that everything depends upon the responsibility of the backward countries themselves. Unless they are ready to stir themselves, unless they are ready to make greater sacrifices, the thing does not start at all.
These men are businessmen. Black has lent nearly $5 billion through the world bank without any loss. That shows the kind of man he is. He is not going around dishing out money for charity. He stresses the need of these countries stirring themselves and developing pride of workmanship and then he goes on to say, which impressed me very much, that the objective should be "that every ounce of resources available is used as efficiently as possible" in these countries. He then had this to say:
And how important it is that the free world community stand ready to pledge whatever measure of its wealth can be usefully employed in this endeavour.
There is the challenge. Let me point out at once the range and the limitations of whatever measure of this wealth can be usefully employed. We are not going to run crazy. The borrowing countries have got to do their part but on the other hand Black suggests that the free world community has a tremendous responsibility. This, as I say, is from an experienced banker who has lent nearly $5 billion without loss.
I have just one other thing to say. I hope that we will not forget the results of failure. If we go on as we are now I think we will fail. I think this thing has got to be stepped up. I should like to refer to some remarks
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
of Adlai Stevenson, for whom I have great respect. He stresses the need of narrowing the economic disparity that exists now in the world. Here are his words:
We can't go on much longer living in a world where, for instance, the average yearly income in America is $2,000 a year and the average yearly income in India is $60.
I remember that I was amazed when I was at the commonwealth conference two years ago over which the Minister of Finance presided; this figure was before us at the time and I was amazed, that there was no complaint on the part of the representative of India. I would not have been a bit surprised if he had said, "Look, we cannot go on this way". But he like Black no doubt was looking at the thing in a practical way. I continue quoting Adlai Stevenson:
No wonder great political, social and scientific revolutions are sweeping the world and that instead of seeing the world go democratic we have seen 11 countries, I think it is, turn to other forms of government in the last few years. Democracy is not winning in the world. It is losing.
You may or may not agree with Stevenson but at any rate we will agree that he has been around and has seen more than most of us have. I admit at once that I was greatly impressed by his statement. He strikes me as being a man with his feet firmly on the ground, and this is what he says. I had not been aware that 11 countries had turned to another form of government.
With regard to our own government, it has given a lead and things have been done. The Minister of Finance has told us about this from time to time and I have quoted the Prime Minister's words which I now repeat:
. Economic assistance to underdeveloped countries/ is a major and mandatory need if freedom is to bei preserved in the world.
I find these words very impressive. I do not think the matter could be put more strongly. My feeling is that people like ourselves should be thinking about it. The Prime Minister will be going to London before long. We do not know what the agenda of the commonwealth conference is but it is pretty hard to believe that the prime ministers will not be thinking about this question. The Prime Minister's words are beginning to carry far, not only as Prime Minister of Canada but also as John Diefen-baker. I should tremendously like to feel that when he goes he may have the feeling that the people of this country are behind him and that if he wants to take great steps in this matter which is all important he will be supported.
Let me emphasize again that there is no intention on the part of people like Hoffman and Black to rush into huge expenditures.

The Budget-Mr. Batten They realize it is going to take years. They realize that the countries to be benefited have got to assume the greatest part of the burden but on the other hand they feel that unless we can steadily improve the situation within a few years the prospect is not going to be good.
My feeling is that it is a fair thing to put this matter before hon. members of the house. I believe that no one should take it lightly and that for unselfish and also for selfish reasons it is a matter of the greatest possible importance that comes right home to every one of us. In my opinion there should be indications given to the Prime Minister and the other members of the government through all kinds of organs of public opinion and by representatives of public opinion, our churches, universities, trade unions, boards of trade and chambers of commerce all across the nation that this matter should be taken seriously.
I suggest that the first people to take it seriously should be ourselves. By what I have said this afternoon and particularly by referring the house to the words of other people I would hope that possibly I have persuaded hon. members that this is a matter which we should all take seriously. We played a great part in the war and I think there is no reason why we should not play an even greater part in peace. I believe that part cries out to be played.

Mr. Speaker, before making any comments dealing directly with the budget I should like to say at this time how grateful I am to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) for his interest and action on behalf of those Newfoundlanders employed on United States air bases in Newfoundland.
I should also like to thank him for his courteous replies to my representations on behalf of those in my own constituency of Humber-St. George's who are employed at the Ernest Harmon air force base in Newfoundland and also for his kind attention to the correspondence from the chairman of the committee representing the employees at this particular base.
In August, 1940, following the establishment of the permanent joint board on defence by the United States and Canada, the United Kingdom, with the approval of the Newfoundland commission of government, gave the United States the right to construct bases in Newfoundland and to hold them on a 99-year lease. Early in 1941 construction began on three chosen sites, namely at St. John's, Argentia and Stephenville. Since the period of initial construction until the present time a number of Canadian citizens have been


employed as full time employees with unlimited tenure. Many of these have been steadily employed for 15 years.
I understand there has been a great deal of correspondence between representative committees appointed by the employees and the commands of the various United States bases, the United States department of defence and the United States civil service commission. I believe also that these agencies have shown considerable interest in the possibility of providing some retirement plan for those "non-citizens holding permanent excepted appointment". The statement made by the minister last Thursday in the house is a most welcome one to all concerned. To those who have worked on this base for some time and who have decided to make their homes in this area the decision with regard to pensions affords a large measure of real satisfaction.
Colonel William H. Noel, the commanding officer at Ernest Harmon air force base, has also shown a keen interest in this retirement plan and has encouraged the committee in their efforts and in their representations. To him I express my appreciation and thanks for adding yet another accomplishment to the long list of services rendered to the people of western Newfoundland by the United States armed forces.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) referred to vocational training. I have a general knowledge of the problem about which he speaks. I think I will say here that education in a broader sense should include not only those in elementary schools, high schools and universities but also those whose abilities lead them toward the technical rather than toward professional fields. I do not want to expand on this problem at this time but I would say that in a country like Canada, which is highly industrialized-and which maybe in the future can look forward to greater industrialization-and a great manufacturing country there will always be the need for technically trained people.
I think that technical education should be expanded all across Canada in order to fit more people for jobs where know-how and native talent are required. In Newfoundland we have a need for this type of education beyond what we already have. But as everybody recognizes, we have great demands on the money allocated for education in my province. At the moment there is a great demand for elementary schools and regional high schools. Then there is the money required to build a new university. All these things add to the burden which the province must bear with regard to its educational responsibilities.

However, from my own correspondence I know that a great deal of interest is being shown in vocational education. Even in my own home city of Corner Brook a well set-up committee is now giving a thorough study to the vocational training act as it applies in Canada and as it would apply in Newfoundland. They are also discussing vocational education as it is operating in Newfoundland. Knowing the personnel of that committee as I do, I have no doubt that when they reach their conclusions those conclusions will be worth studying.
I come now to a brief consideration of the budget. During the last few months we have heard, both inside and outside of this house, that this government has no financial policy, that it has failed to provide the leadership which Canadians expect and that it operates on the theory that time solves most problems by removing them. There is a good deal of truth in that statement and the best evidence of it is the budget of 1960. In his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) gave a report of the year's operations and then after a little bit of sermonizing he expressed the hope that during the coming year everything would turn out for the best. The trade deficit, tight money, unemployment, defence spending and many other topics of daily interest to our people were touched on only lightly or ignored altogether.
During the election campaigns of 1957 and 1958 the present government pledged itself to lower taxes, lower spending and lower interest rates. According to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in 1957 every Canadian was overtaxed by $30 a year and every family was overtaxed by $120 a year. He said that the government of the day was on a wild spending spree and that high interest rates and tight money were forcing industry, the provinces and the municipalities to the wall. Then he shouted, "Give us a chance, we will show you". The Canadian people gave him the chance. Let us now have a look at some of the results of his stewardship.
The revenues of this country in 1957 amounted to $5,106 million and in 1960 to $5,892 million. This means that the average per capita revenue in 1957 was $314 and in 1960, $334 or an increase of $20. Rather than taxes being reduced by 20 per cent, the per capita tax in the last three years has been increased by approximately $20.
Let us look at expenditures. Expenditures in 1957 was $4,849 million, an average of $295 per person. In 1960 the estimated expenditure is $5,880 million, an average of $334 per person. Here the per capita expenditure is shown to be $40 more than it was in the year '57.
The Budget-Mr. Batten
Our net debt was $11 billion in 1957; in 1960 it was $12,100 million. In 1957 the average net debt was $664 per person; in 1960 it was $681 per person, an increase of $17.
In 1957 the net interest on our national debt was $313 million; in 1960 the net interest on our national debt was $499 million. In 1957 the net interest as a percentage of our debt was 2.85 per cent; in 1960 it was 4.13 per cent. Interest rates were less than 4 per cent during the election campaign of 1957; in August of last year they were well over 6 per cent.
The minister went on last year in his budget speech to say that he expected that the gross national product would increase by 7 per cent. We now know that his expectations were not fullfilled.
Fifty per cent wrong in volume.

The increase in the gross national product is no more, and may be a good deal less, than during a number of the years under Liberal administration. I am not going to give the figures on all this because they have been given by other speakers. The figure of borrowings was $164 million in 1958, $1,200 million in 1959 and $900 million in 1960, making a total volume of $2.3 billion odd.
Obviously this government has been on a wild spending spree of unequalled proportions. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) a few moments ago referred to the fact that the government was now paying its way. I do not think the government is paying its way until it is able to repay to the Canadian people the money which it has borrowed from them in the last three years and then has brought forth a balanced budget. I do not think this government will be in power long enough to pay the expenses of this exhibition of, or expedition into, Toryism.
In the matter of trade, we have a trade deficit of $1,460 million. All these items go to show the manner in which the present government has kept its promises to the Canadian people. I remember that in 1957 the Prime Minister shouted, "Take the tax-masters off the backs of the Canadian people". Who are the taxmasters now? Surely when we look at these figures we must realize that these promises must have been made in days when the government did not have the responsibility it has now.
We talk about tight money and interest rates. The Prime Minister talked about them in 1957 and pointed out how damaging they were to the provinces and the municipalities.

The Budget-Mr. Batten He went on to take credit in 1958 for lowering the interest rate, yet in 1959 he disclaimed all responsibility for tight money or high interest rates. Let us look at what the Prime Minister said in 1958. In Calgary on March 14 of that year he claimed that interest rates had fallen sharply as a result of government action since the previous June, from a high of 4.33 per cent to 2.89 per cent. Surely if the government can reduce inerest rates in 1957 it can reduce interest rates in 1959.
He went on to outline in Selkirk on March 17, 1958, as reported in the Toronto Telegram of March 18, Progressive Conservative accomplishments since they had assumed office, and he declared that one of these was to ease the tight money situation inherited from the former Liberal administration. If the Prime Minister and his cabinet eased tight money in 1957, then they did not think they had the authority and responsibility and the know-how to do it in 1959.
When the Tories are out of power the Liberals are blamed for tight money and high interest rates. When the Tories are in power they disclaim all responsibility and place that responsibility on the Bank of Canada and the chartered banks. When the Tories are out, the government of the day is the villain; when the Tories are in the government the Bank of Canada is the whipping boy. When the Tories are out they see one side of the penny; but when the Tories are in they flip the "Coyne".
When the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) spoke yesterday I did not think he was completely satisfied. He made reference to the appointment of a minister for Atlantic affairs. This is what he said, as reported on page 2926 of Hansard:
-perhaps the time has arrived when there should be appointed a minister of Atlantic affairs just as we have a minister of northern affairs.
I could not agree with a statement like that. In the first place the position of the provinces is quite different from that of the Northwest Territories. Again, I would have some very grave doubts about appointing a minister for Atlantic affairs, because all that would do would be to make a colonial office for the Atlantic provinces. I do not think the Atlantic premiers are very happy about it either.
I have here a page taken from today's Montreal Gazette, which contains an article headed "Regional monetary policy". Perhaps the Minister of Finance would listen to this. Then there is a subheading, "Atlantic premiers ask British banker's aid".
The Minister of Finance should listen to this.

It goes on:
The Atlantic provinces premiers have asked one of Britain's foremost bankers to study the effect of federal money policies on the Atlantic region, it was learned here. Sir Oliver Franks, chairman of Lloyds Bank, told them he would consider their request and give an answer in about 19 days.
Would the hon. member permit me to suggest that he ought to speak possibly with a little more force so that the Minister of Finance, who is now engaged, could listen to this very important subject.

It continues:
It is understood Franks has been asked to head a commission of three who would investigate the effect of Ottawa's money policies at first hand and submit recommendations or changes.
Surely this indicates that the premiers of the Atlantic provinces are not very happy with the monetary policy of the present government.
Going back to some of the promises which have been made by the Tory party, one can almost see the sky darkened by the flapping wings of chickens coming home to roost. Or we could look back over the long list of Tory promises on which this government was elected and, viewing them in the light of accomplishments, is it any wonder that the government should want to scorn the base degrees by which they did ascend.

speechtext: The best record in history.

You will have a job to prove it. I come now to a few comments concerning civil service salaries. For many months the government has had this question under consideration, but the shabby treatment accorded to members of the civil service last Thursday evening compounded all that was done before. Determination of civil service salaries is a joint responsibility of the civil service commission and the government as outlined in section 11 of the Civil Service Act. Generally the policy of the federal government has been to relate increases in salary to the remuneration received by workers in comparable fields. This policy was well defined in 1951 by the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, when he said:
As I have said on previous occasions, the government's policy in these matters is based on two main principles, first, that salary and pay scales and other conditions of employment in both the civil service and the armed forces should be such as to attract and retain persons of the right type and necessary qualifications; second, that having regard to aneilliary conditions of employment, remuneration for each class of work or employment should be generally in line with that paid for comparable work by good private employers.

On May 1, 1958, the Prime Minister expressed the same view in these words:
For many years it has been generally accepted that two main principles should guide the determination of salaries in the service. First, the salaries must be enough to do the job, that is, to attract enough of the right kind of men and women into the service and keep them in it. Second, they must be fair as between civil servants and people outside the service-the taxpayers-which means that the salaries we pay for any class of work should be comparable with those paid by private employers for similar classes of work taking into account the other terms of employment that are necessary to make a fair comparison. I think these principles should continue to guide us.
In an effort to arrive at some satisfactory method of comparing civil service salaries with those in other fields the government in September, 1957 set up a pay research bureau following a similar development in the United Kingdom a year earlier. This bureau, under the direction of the civil service commission and the Department of Finance, made its first report which was followed by a report of the commission in the spring of 1958 stating that no general revision of salaries was warranted. At that time the government refused the request for salary increases and shifted the blame from the shoulders of the cabinet to the commission by tabling the report in the House of Commons. This report was not embarrassing to the government, because it could be used to support the cabinet's rejection of the civil service request, a rejection based on the government's financial position which had been brought about by the government's own financial ineptitude.
Further investigation was made by the bureau, and it was shown that some classes were receiving salaries 20 per cent below those paid by private employers. The overall picture revealed a gap of about 8 per cent. The commission's report based on these findings was not tabled in the House of Commons although it had been received about six weeks before the last session ended. Why was the 1959 report not tabled? Why was it considered to be confidential although the 1958 report had been made public? Obviously on this occasion the government could not use the commission as a whipping boy. Responsibility for the denial was now placed squarely in the lap of the government. Then, true to form, the government began its delaying tactics and returned the report for further examination.
Finally, on Friday, October 13-it was a most unlucky Friday for the civil service- the Minister of Finance flatly denied to accord the increases. This time, having no commission report to support his action, he proceeded immediately to muster public opinion and backing by stating that the
The Budget-Mr. Batten salary raises which had been requested would cost $214 million which would be equivalent to an increase of 15 per cent in the income tax rates. One can hardly conceive of a more effective statement with regard to placing public opinion behind the minister's rejection and militating against a favourable attitude on the part of the taxpayers toward the civil servants' application.
The arithmetic by which the minister began with $50 million to meet an 8 per cent increase in salary and concluded with $242 million is devious and doubtful. The minister may not have intended to do so, but he certainly left the impression in the public mind that if the requested increases were granted the total amount would be an immediate charge on the treasury for the year 1959. The public may take a different view and consider that if almost $6 billion is to be collected by the Minister of Finance the spending of this money, while directed by the government, should be managed by those who are qualified to do so and who are sufficiently well paid to do so.
A few months ago the increases requested by the civil service were supposed to cost $242 million. In the next budget speech the minister stated that $15 million would be sufficient to provide increases for about one-third of the civil service. No wonder there is confusion and resentment. This whole matter has been poorly handled by the government. The arrogant manner in which the recommendations of the civil service commission were rejected; the minister's tabling of one report when it suited his purpose-

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Finance wants to talk I prefer that he do so in his own time. I would remind the house that there are three kinds of politicians, those who talk too much, those who tax too much and those exceptions who do both. The Minister of Finance is the exception.
In discussing these salaries I agree with the minister's class by class arrangement which I am sure will be welcomed by the civil servants but I am sure they will be concerned with the date of this revision and the date from which any increase will be effective. Certainly this revision was in the mind of the minister when he presented his budget. Why was the announcement not made then? Obviously, to the Minister of Finance a headline in the daily papers indicating a surplus was more important than the peace of mind of the civil servants.
I wish now to refer to the speech made on Tuesday last by my friend the hon. member for York-Sunbury. The hon. gentleman placed a table on the record at page 2925 of Hansard showing the amount of money spent under different headings in the years 1955 and 1959. There is some question in my mind as to why the hon. gentleman should pick the year 1955. I believe that if comparisons


are to be made they should be made between significant years. Why not take the year 1945 or 1935?
The hon. gentleman then went on to give the amount of money being spent under different headings and referred, for example, to the trans-Canada highway. There has been no money spent by this government on the trans-Canada highway except that which would normally follow the initial legislation. The government has brought in no legislation to amend the act other than to provide the money that is normally required.
My hon. friend then went on to speak about the amount of money given to the Atlantic provinces for the acquisition of buildings and vessels. The question that comes to my mind is this. What about the 50 ships that were going to form the nucleus of a great Canadian mercantile fleet? What about the Canadian steamships down in Halifax harbour? Statements of this kind are wild and unfounded.
I am reminded of the occasion when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) claimed that his government built the airport at Stephen-ville. That airport was constructed, had been officially opened and was being used before the election of 1957. I am also reminded of a statement made by the Prime Minister last November in the famous speech when he spoke about social justice and referred to the increases which had been given to the Canadian people under the heading of family allowances. I am sure the Canadian people have received no increases under the heading of family allowances as a result of any legislative action on the part of this government.
Oh?
None whatever.
Indeed, none whatever.
They got promises, but nothing else before then.

I turn to the speech made by the Minister of Finance in Halifax, I believe last October. He referred to a number of things in the Atlantic provinces and although I do not believe he intended to do so directly he certainly left with the people to whom he was speaking the impression that these things were Conservative policies.
He referred, for example, to the feed freight assistance policy and went on to describe how important it was to the maritime provinces. It certainly is important but I know that this policy was initiated by the Liberal government in 1941. He went on to

talk about the great benefits derived by the Atlantic provinces from the industrial development bank. That, too, came into being as a result of Liberal legislation passed in 1944.
The hon. gentleman went on further to talk about the Atlantic provinces' adjustment grants. Here I am going to give the minister full marks. I have said both inside this house and outside of it, and I shall say again, that in providing these special grants to the Atlantic provinces the minister has done a commendable job for which I give him full credit. He made reference to those grants in his speech on that occasion.
The hon. gentleman also referred to the subventions on coal, yet coal subventions were started in 1928, a year when a Liberal government was in power in this country. The minister's next reference is a dandy. He referred to the $15 million paid by the federal government toward the construction of the Canso causeway. Here again is a good Liberal project.
The hon. gentleman went on to talk about Camp Gagetown, another project initiated by the Liberal government. He spoke about the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act passed in 1944, the Farm Improvement Loans Act also passed in that year and also referred to freight rates in the maritime provinces stating that money had been granted to reduce the rates in those provinces, but they were reduced to 10 per cent from 17 per cent after the rates had been increased.
The minister when making his speech would have been more interesting to the people in the Atlantic provinces if he had made reference to special income tax concessions to industry locating there, if he had talked about the freight rate structure in the Atlantic provinces, low cost capital loans, consideration for the building of trunk highways, a greater allocation of defence spending and the tariff structure in relation to the maritimes. Those are things in which the people there are interested. However, we do give him credit for giving to the people of the maritimes a long list of Liberal accomplishments.
I turn now to a consideration of federal-provincial relations. We all know the story here. We know that during the 1957 election campaign the Prime Minister promised that if he were elected his government would call a federal-provincial conference immediately to settle some of the problems existing between the provincial governments and the senior government of this country. He said, for example, on April 25, 1957, in his opening campaign speech in Massey Hall:
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring
The Budget-Mr. Mandziuk
about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government, but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect.
In the same speech he said:
-a Conservative government, if elected, would immediately call a federal-provincial conference to settle existing problems.
I could cite a number of these references, but let us examine what has happened. A conference was called late in November. The premiers came, made their statements and went home with the promise of another meeting in January. No such meeting was ever called.
