Mr. Speaker, it was a pleasure to hear such enlightening addresses from the members of the opposition; it was a pleasure to hear political battles fought over again today; it was a pleasure to hear how many people are unhappy and in particular those sitting on the benches opposite. I felt that there might be some change in this world but yet it has not changed. The life and activity of this nation, both in production and development, are going on at a great pace in spite of the fact that the "experienced" hands of the gentlemen opposite are not at the helm of state. Because they are not at the helm of state they resort to every trick known to oratory to introduce doubt and timidity in the public mind. Do we need any proof of this statement? Just glance back at what has been going on during this session, during the last few months, few weeks or few days.
Not so long ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) gave us a very interesting and exhaustive review of the situation of Canadian trade. Canadians were happy to hear	that our	export trade	wasexpanding,	that	we were	gaining new markets. But,	Mr.	Speaker,	this stunned	theopposition	for	a while.	Then when	they
regained their balance they charged him with too much optimism. "Oh, you are too optimistic. Things are not as good as you say. Oh, how much better they would be if we were sitting there instead of the place where the Canadian people put us."
I was going to make reference to a critical editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press. In view of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce rose this afternoon on a question of privilege, it is already on the record and I am going to skip it.
Let us go to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green). Most of the country thinks he has done a wonderful job.

The Budget-Mr. Mandziuk In spite of the fact that he is not as experienced as some of those men opposite, a lot of those experienced men opposite have their former colleagues at home biting their fingernails. Hon. members know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs spoke with pride of the role Canada is playing in world affairs, e.g. in the United Nations. This role is nothing to blush about. Canada's role and influence in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, in the British commonwealth of nations and in international affairs is probably out of proportion to our size and population. This role is owing to the leadership that our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) has given.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs gave us the exact picture. What did we hear from the opposition? Oh, they joined in a chorus: You are too optimistic; Oh, this world is so dark; there are dark clouds on the horizon, thunder and lightning; hell will break loose unless the Canadian people realize that they have been fooled. Do they know why they are where they are? They are there because they fooled the Canadian people until they realized it.
I think the review of the Secretary of State for External Affairs filled us with pride. I think any person with any sense should appreciate criticism. I could refer to the words of President Eisenhower when he spoke to one of the Latin American nations, either Argentina or Brazil. He said, "We are not saints; we can make mistakes, but our hearts are in the right place." Are the hearts of these people who criticize in the right place? What do we hear from them? "Disarm, disarm", one section cries. "Oh, to arms, to arms", the other section cries. They accuse us of lack of leadership. I am trying to give the house my personal reactions, the reactions that I get as a backbencher, as a man with no political experience, the reaction I get from all this back-biting back and forth.
Let us go to another department. If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had any secret hopes that he would get any bouquets or prizes for bringing in a balanced budget he must be disappointed. When the minister budgeted for a deficit in previous years the hue and cry was: "You are driving this country into ruin; oh, you are spending money like a drunken sailor." Hon. members heard that, did they not? It was said, "You are spendthrifts; you are leading us into inflation that is going to be the ruin of this country. What does he know about finance?"
Who is that?

I am just repeating the words and the questions that they asked and the implications that they tried to put across


to the people of this country. But, when the minister brings in a balanced budget they call it "cold porridge". That is what the expert financial critic said. They call it, "a do-nothing budget, a don't-budge budget; they say that the jobless were ignored", and so on down the line.
In the course of my remarks I shall give some of the reactions of the Canadian Press. But before I do so, I want to mention the criticism, or the so-called criticism, as it affected me. When interest rates were going up last summer we heard nothing more than the theme, "tight money, tight money". We even had some questions on the orders of the day. What are they saying today when interest rates are going down? There is not a peep from the other side. Why?
They are all asleep.
Oh, yes. It will be a long time before they wake up.
We are enjoying your speech; it is very good.

Thank you. I am giving it for your enjoyment. Let me refer to another department. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) was all but crucified, all but charged with treason, when under his instruction, direction and leadership the stabilization board changed the system of price supports on eggs and pork from outright purchase to deficiency payments. What did we hear in this house?
The hon. member for Ros-thern.

Blue ruin. Barrels and barrels of tears were shed for the poor farmers. I too felt like crying for them because I knew they were not getting a square deal. But why the silence now? The Minister of Agriculture asked the house and the country to give the scheme a chance and I am beginning to think that the minister has some horse sense. Egg prices are going up and the opposition has not asked one single egg question or one omelet question up to this time. But I think that wonderful troupe is tuning up for a new chorus. There will be another chorus. Do you know what it is going to be? When the price of eggs reaches a certain level, a level of prices to which I think Canadian farmers are entitled, the opposition is going to be singing another chorus. In whose defence will they be crying? They will be saying that the poor consumer is going to suffer because the price of eggs is going up. They cry, they always cry.
I have tried to follow the criticism of the budget. I like to hear objective criticism.

We appreciate that. But all we hear are bits here and bits there. Do you remember the story-I think some hon. members will- about the six blind men of Hindustan who went to see the elephant. Each one touched a certain part of the elephant. The one who touched the ear said that the elephant was like a fan. The fellow who took hold of the elephant's tail said that it was like a whip or rope; he could not be convinced otherwise. The chap who got hold of the elephant's front leg said that it was very much like a tree. But the fellow who bumped his head against the body said that the elephant was like a wall. Then they started to fight among themselves as to who was right. That is what we get by way of criticism from the opposition.
Those of us who lack the political experience of the gentlemen in the opposition are astounded and bewildered by such tactics. But we have some common sense and common sense tells us that the aim of the opposition is to talk the country into another recession so that they can be given an opportunity to put on their tarnished and battered armour, get out their three-legged horse and pose as saviours of the people in the next election. If you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read an extract from a newspaper article. How true are the words written by Nate White in the Christian Science Monitor of February 20 last. Mr. White is the business and financial editor of this paper and this is what he had to say under the headline, "Gloom-Talk Hobbles U.S. Boom". The article refers to the United States but I think it is most applicable to Canada. He said:
A recession does not begin solely from talk, but talk plays an important part in it. Talk becomes publicity, and publicity in this highly communicative society multiplies. It Is extremely easy to manufacture a recession almost literally out of thin air once the communication system gets in motion. This is what is happening now.
He is referring to the United States but that is what is happening right in this country and in this house. He went on to say:
But if gloom, like a low-spreading fog, continues to creep throughout the nation, it can introduce doubts and timidity in public thought and eventually in business decisions. Before anyone hardly knows what has happened, a recession is upon us.
This must be the object of the opposition. The words of this eminent journalist are so applicable to the tactics and apparent plans of these people who were so long in power and so used to ruling this country that like children they are still crying for those sweet days when they were in power.
The Budget-Mr. Mandziuk
The budget has been introduced and the rules call for a maximum of eight days debate. Barrels and barrels of tears will be shed. In fact, several barrels of tears have been shed already. Eight days of debate costs the Canadian taxpayers a pretty penny. Therefore Canadians expect their elected representatives to give full and careful consideration to the manner in which the government raises money and the manner in which it spends it. The budget has been labelled as a cold porridge, do-nothing budget and everything else, but I maintain that it will have definite effects on every segment of our economy.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

As we adjourned at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, one of my colleagues remarked on the fact that our friends, the Grits, were conspicuous by their absence, there being one frontbencher and two or three others present. But I was heartened by another colleague who said that when their leader teed off with a non-confidence motion on Monday, I think it was, with a very good factual criticism of our defence policy, he counted only 13 of his supporters during that one speech of his. I was therefore heartened. I have not lost heart. I was reflecting that they did not care to listen to an inconspicuous backbencher and that was the reason they had stayed away.
I hope the hon. member has better arguments than that one.

I am again reminded of the six blind men of Hindustan by this remark of my friend.
Taking the budget as a whole we should be happy, if for nothing else than the fact that there are no tax increases. I join those who have spoken previously in complimenting the Minister of Finance on a job well done. Hon. members do not need to take my word for it. I know in particular that members of the opposition often resort to opinions appearing in the press. May I be permitted to quote from the Winnipeg Tribune an editorial published on April 1, the day after the budget was presented. It states in part as follows:
Just the same, the budget must have given many Canadians a great deal of quiet satisfaction. For the first time since 1957 the finances of the country were climbing out of the red into the black. Mr. Fleming was able to balance the 1960-61 budget and even forecast a small surplus.
This means-

The Budget-Mr. Mandziuk
I hope the doubting Thomases will take this into account.
-that the inflationary effects of government fiscal operations should diminish considerably and that the competition for capital resulting from heavy federal government borrowing should ease off. This year Ottawa will borrow only $201 million compared with $900 million in 1959. The provinces and private agencies should be able to borrow for more of their growth needs in Canada rather than being forced into the U.S. money market.
I quote further:
The effects of this determination, and effort are already being felt.
I ask my hon. friends to mark these words.
The bank rate-a barometer of tension in the nation's finances-has fallen to 3.26 per cent-
No wonder they do not ask how the bank rates are at the present time.
-after a steady eight-week decline.
Mr. Fleming is further complimented in this editorial as follows:
The essence of Mr. Fleming's budget speech and the budget itself was middle-of-the-road moderation. The same can hardly be said for the initial criticism of the budget by William Benidickson, Liberal financial critic. It is his job to criticize and to tear budgets apart, but statements like "shocker" and "I don't know when a country has lost so much ground in so short a time" simply detract from a serious opposition assessment of the government's financial shortcomings.
That is the opinion of an extremely responsible paper. I recollect that the other day-I think it was on Tuesday-this same hon. gentleman, namely the financial critic of the official opposition, appeared on television and was asked what he would do. His answer, as probably those who saw that broadcast are aware, was this, "We would consult experts and we would do something". They had time in which to do something for a good many years.
However I should like to come nearer home and come to the capital. May I be permitted to quote a bit from the Ottawa Journal dated April 1, the day after the budget was introduced? It states as follows:
This is Mr. Fleming's answer to the pessimists who, within the past two years, saw deficit spending bringing possible budget deficits of a billion dollars, spoke of mounting debt and inflation threatening fiscal ruin.
The Jeremiahs who talked that way forgot Donald Fleming; forgot the Calvinistic finance minister who knew his stuff and did his homework and had the courage to say "no". The man who said "no" on civil service salaries-
Although they threatened to jump through the roof, as one hon. gentleman has remarked. They should attend to their business in offices instead of trying to jump through roofs away out west.
-said "no" to his ministerial colleagues, said "no" in the treasury board. Come hell or high water, the line would be held.


That is Donald Fleming as described in the Ottawa Journal. The editorial goes on to say this about the minister's estimates:
Hopeful guesses? Perhaps; but Mr. Fleming's past guesses have been amazingly good-his estimate a year ago of national income and the deficit came within fractions of being right.
In any event, come what may short of war, pestilence or other catastrophe, we have left big deficit budgets behind, for the time being at any rate; have struck our fiscal tents, with promise of prosperity ahead.
That is the local paper. I know the charge may come forth that these two papers that a backbencher has quoted are always favourable to the Tories but how about quoting from a paper which is favourable to the Grits? An extremely eminent journalist, who at least has grit tendencies with a small "g", namely John Bird, writing in the Toronto Star, stated this. May I quote part of his article? I respect the gentleman's judgment because I believe he showed good judgment when he was writing this article. Here is what he says:
However, the budget itself does bring Canada some way toward meeting the conditions which Coyne lays down-
Although very reluctantly, he still admits something, does he not? I continue the quotation:
-namely a reduction in the rate of our increasing dependence on foreign financing. It's roundabout, but it's there.
That is important. I do not care how the minister obtains it but he has obtained it. I come back to the quotation:
More important even than a small budgetary balance is the cut-back in estimated "cash requirements", that is in the need for the government to borrow money outside. For the coming year cash requirements for which the government will have to go to the money market are estimated at only $201 million as against $900 million last year and $1,273 million the year before.
That indicates that there is a very favourable reaction to this year's budget. Time does not permit, but I could quote for hours from various papers across the country showing a favourable response to this budget, this "cold porridge budget". True, some items show concern. I think we are here for the purpose of giving every item in the budget our serious consideration. I will share with you, Mr. Speaker, what disturbs me, and that is the statement by the Minister of Finance that the tariff was going to be increased on textiles.
Textiles immediately made me think of Japan. What effect would these tariff increases have on our trade with that country? I am going to paraphrase the minister's remarks he made to the Saskatchewan board of trade on February 19. He said that we westerners are very touchy at the mention of anything that may endanger disposal of our

wheat, because next to the United Kingdom Japan has become our second best customer for this product of the soil. Japan purchased $70 million worth in 1959. Western Canada depends so much on this country buying our foodstuffs.
I can well recall letters written by farm leaders from the west at the news that there were some negotiations going on between this government and the government of Japan about the cut-back on some of the imports coming in from that friendly country. The farm organizations were very disturbed and wrote letters to the Prime Minister and to the government. This same subject occupied a lot of space in the briefs presented by the interprovincial farm union as well as in the brief presented by the union federation of agriculture.
I myself was disturbed and wanted to find out what was the situation in fact, and I found the answer in the minister's address to the Saskatchewan board of trade on February 19 of this year. I would advise those hon. gentlemen who have not read this address to do so, because I think it throws a lot of light on this matter and it enlightened me about some of these matters which really disturbed me. I quote from this address, page 18:
There are two particular features of the agreement which are noteworthy. The first is the escape clause whereby Canada reserves the right to apply fixed values for duty in the event of damage to Canadian industry: the second, the provision for consultation whereby each country undertook to give sympathetic consideration to representations made by the other. You should know that in the six years which have elapsed since the signing of the trade agreement with Japan, Canada has not once resorted to this special escape clause. We have been able to resolve our problems through frank and friendly consultations. This is the way of friends, and I assure you that both Canada and Japan would very much like to continue in this spirit of friendly co-operation.
That shows the basis of agreement between us and Japan. We know for a fact that in 1959 Japanese exports to Canada amounted to $105 million; $25 million of those Japanese imports, one quarter, were textiles. They affected our textile industry; I realize that.
But as a good friend and customer, Japan imposes restraints on exports to Canada. That is in accordance with the terms of the treaty. She recognizes that exports to Canada must proceed gradually and that she must avoid a disruption of Canadian markets. Japan recognizes that she must avoid excesses or flooding of Canadian markets with any one particular commodity.
I had to have two questions answered to be satisfied in my mind that the textile industry in Canada was an industry of sufficient importance, because we of the west, the
The Budget-Mr. Mandziuk woolly west, do not recognize the importance of some of these industries to Canada. I looked at the Canada Year Book and I found some very interesting facts, although the Canada Year Book of 1959 only contains statistics and records for 1956. But I found that there were 3,776 textile, clothing and woollen mills employing almost 200,000 people. That is a good sized industry.
Then I went further and searched to see whether there was any such animal in Manitoba, that young province which entered confederation in 1870. To my surprise I found that Manitoba had 37 textile mills, four knitting mills and 154 clothing establishments. This industry employed around 7,000 people. All in all there is around 200,000 people employed, and that means that if every family has an average of three or four members, there are about 800,000 human beings who depend for their bread and butter on work in our textile industry.
That impressed me because of the fact that this government recognized the importance of the agricultural industry. Therefore, the simple answer is, why not recognize the importance of the textile industry? If it gives a living to almost one million people in Canada, why should it not receive some consideration? This government has given consideration to improving the conditions of the agricultural industry by various enactments, such as farm improvement legislation, farm credit, acreage payments, cash advances, price stabilization, and shared assistance to farmers to compensate them for grain snowed under.
I had, too, another question which should be answered, because I realize we have to keep our people employed. Will this increase in tariff rates endanger our trade with Japan? I am watching the clock, Mr. Speaker, and I could quote from the address of the Minister of Finance, as reported in Hansard at pages 681 and 682 of February 3 last. I could read extracts from his address in Saskatoon at page 20, but time does not permit.
There it is shown that our trade with Japan is on the increase, that in the three months of November, December and January just past it has gone up. That is very encouraging. I am glad the Japanese understand that we cannot permit an influx in large volume of any particular manufactured product, because what Japan sends to us are finished manufactured products which compete with products made in Canada, while we sell to them raw products, foodstuffs, wheat, or products of the mine and of the soil. But having asked these two questions, I think I can safely meet with very little fear any

The Budget-Mr. Herridge criticism by farmers out west and prove to them that this industry was entitled to this recommendation of the tariff board. It was not a decision of one man but of the whole board. It deserves some consideration.
In closing, I should like to give a few words of warning, not to the minister, because I think he is doing his best, but to industry. I hope the textile industry does not take this as a licence or as an excuse for raising the prices of their products. I hope that labour does not take this as a licence to ask for, and strike for higher wages. The Minister of Finance has asked us to hold the line. He is asking everyone to hold the line, including the big corporations.
As a man who grew up and grew old out in the west, I can say that this price squeeze in which the farmer finds himself caught today is the result of rising costs. I should like to read in the press that there has been a cutback in the profits made by the corporation, profits which in some cases have reached astronomical figures. This is what is causing the price squeeze. I do not attribute to labour, in the main, the causes for these rising prices. I believe that our labour is efficient. I believe that for a dollar's worth of work our labour produces more than any other labour on earth. But I feel everyone must cooperate. This appeal made by the Minister of Finance to all of us to hold the line applies to the corporations, also.
I wish to repeat that the reason we are being priced out of the markets of the world, and the cause of this price squeeze, is rising costs. I am prepared to grant tariff protection but, again, I say I hope industry does not take this tariff protection as licence. We have to get our labour working but we also have to be prepared to compete with goods coming from Japan or from any other country. Of course, we want to trade with Japan as well, because trade is a two-way street.
In closing I should like to quote the words of the Minister of Finance as they appear on the official record of this house:
So long as our access to foreign markets is unimpaired and we are able to keep the cost and the quality of our products and services thoroughly competitive we need have no fear for the future.
I think that applies to everyone. It applies to big business, small business and everyone alike.

I rise to support the subamendment, and in order to relate it directly to my remarks I should like to quote it again at this time:
That the amendment be amended by striking out the period after the word "unemployment" and adding thereto the following words:


'and in the opinion of this house the solution of these problems requires amongst other things that the government give consideration to the following measures:
1.	The planned elimination of wasteful defence expenditures,
2.	The provision of a self-liquidating public investment program,
3.	The provision of an appropriate capital gains
tax.'
Before proceeding with my remarks, I do want to say that I enjoyed a number of the speeches which have been made by hon. members in this debate on both sides of the house. Whether I agree with them or not, I like people to get up and express themselves and tell the house where they stand-although I must say we are decidedly under the impression before they rise that we know where they stand.
I was particularly interested in the very thoughtful speech which was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) especially when he referred to the international situation and the contest going on in the world today; the struggle of ideas between those who believe in democratic institutions and those who are supporting forms of dictatorship.
I listened carefully and with interest to the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I have listened to the minister for 12 years as a pessimist in this house, and three years as an optimist. I listened very carefully the other evening when the minister was speaking, with his Cromwellian stance, preaching the doctrines of Gladston-ianism, doctrines of retrenchment and reform in the nugatory accents of Bay street.
While I was listening to the hon. gentleman I was inclined to think of past days, and I was reminded how much the minister resembled in his ideas and his mannerisms a very old friend of mine, an old Kootenay pioneer. As soon as I mention that magic word "Kootenay" I see all faces turned this way as if I was about to open the doors to paradise. Anyway, he was an excellent person. He performed the role of a minor tax collector and collected money due for mining licences, fishing licences, dog licences, and that sort of thing. He was a scion of the house of Buccleuch in Scotland. He was a Presbyterian elder, a man of unquestioned integrity, untainted virtue and as stubborn as a mule. He had another interesting facet to his character. He flew a Union Jack in front of his premises every day and, as a matter of fact, he had a Union Jack always on one desk or table in his office. I have heard of someone else who had a Union Jack draped on his desk in this house. But, as I said before, he was an excellent character, a lifetime friend

of mine who combined in his person all the characteristics of John Knox and Scrooge.
His family motto was: Always balance the budget. He was known as Walter Balance the Budget. I will illustrate what a good chancellor of the exchequer he was in his official capacity and in his domestic affairs, too. I remember being in a post office on one occasion when he went in to post some papers. He used to send the Vancouver newspaper to his brother in Australia. He handed the paper in, and the postmaster handed it back and said: It is a cent short. It will take another cent stamp.
He looked at him for a moment. "Ah, my boy," he said, "hand it me back, I'll take it home and cut out the advertisements." He promptly walked home, took an hour or so to cut out the advertisements, walked back and mailed the paper. Naturally he was a Conservative. Why I was reminded of this gentleman when the minister was speaking is because he always believed in balancing the budget. It is always wise to do so so far as the current account or daily or annual consumption is concerned, but to be successful as chancellor of the exchequer you must do more. You must have fiscal policies that make the best use of the human and natural resources you have in the country.
This old gentleman was well off in natural resources. He owned miles of timber limits and a good number of mineral claims which he never developed because he would always insist on balancing the budget and would not develop them until he had accumulated sufficient surplus so to do and he never accumulated that surplus. He died after 50 years of waiting for a surplus without having developed his resources because he wanted to balance the budget and was not willing to secure credit based on his natural resources or undertake a self-liquidating enterprise in the interest of the country.
When the minister was speaking I could not help but think of this ancient friend and very fine gentleman because in many respects I think the minister resembles him. We can learn a lesson from the faults of this humble chancellor of the exchequer and so can our present chancellor of the exchequer. I want it understood that my comments are directed to the minister in his official capacity because as a private citizen I know he is one of the kindest men who has ever picked the pockets of a helpless taxpayer.
I realize that the minister has to budget within the terms of reference of the capitalist system which provides certain limitations. My criticisms and the alternatives I propose to government budgeting are based on the
79951-0-191
The Budget-Mr. Herridge socialist philosophy and outlook which of course means that instead of placing profits first we must consider humanity first.
We live in an expanding economy producing an abundance for all and exporting large quantities of goods. We have the abundance but what do we have against that? At the lowest estimate, the one accepted by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), we have at the present time approximately one half million unemployed. That is the situation facing us. Unemployment is a serious and continuing problem in all its various aspects whether it is seasonal, occupational, regional, structural, technological or otherwise. This is a serious disease of modern capitalist society.
Anyone who reads books or daily, weekly or monthly publications knows there is an increasing interest on the part of economists in this aspect of modern society, continuing unemployment regardless of the prosperity of the majority.
To support my argument I shall quote a few brief paragraphs from an article by Edwin Copps which appeared in Saturday Night, issue of April 2, 1960. He writes what I consider a helpful article on the subject entitled "The Stubborn Facts About Unemployment" which appeared under the heading "Ottawa Letter":
One of the minor tragedies of parliamentary battles is that their most important aspects are quickly forgotten. Politics creates most of its clamour about trifles. People remember the points that don't matter and miss the points that do.
There is much truth in that. I continue:
For example, if Canadians remember anything about the most recent debate on unemployment it will be that most of the squabbling was about figures. They will recall that the opposition claims that nearly 900,000 persons were unemployed this winter while the government believes half a million were without work and looking for it.
That depends upon which side of the house you sit. I continue:
This bickering masks the main malignancy of our economic life. It is the fact that our nation has within it a tumour that won't go away. It is a hard nub of persistent unemployment, a continuing surplus of labour in some parts of Canada. In good times and bad, it would appear, we have less than "full employment".
In the rare moments of enlightenment when it was not gazing at two sets of troublesome figures, like a snake before the beady eyes of a mongoose, the House of Commons saw clearly something it was loath to admit. What it saw was this: we only enjoy full employment in wartime. At other times, even relatively prosperous ones like the present, many of our people are either on relief or sipping at the weak brew provided by unemployment insurance benefits.
Regardless of which side of the house we sit on I think as realists trying to find solutions to the difficult problems that face us- and no one suggests there is an overnight

The Budget-Mr. Herridge solution-we must recognize the disease. In this case the disease is continuing unemployment in some of the sectors of modern society.
At the same time we realize as this problem exists we find various veterans organizations urging a 33J per cent increase in the pensions of disability pensioners. Simultaneously, the veterans organizations urge an improvement in war veterans allowances particularly with respect to permissive income and some other aspects of war veterans allowance legislation. These increases are requested by organizations that are in close touch with veterans because they realize the people concerned require some adjustment in the pensions or allowances they receive to meet the changing cost of living in recent years.
We also find that many of our senior citizens lack the necessities of life and simple comforts. I have had the opportunity to visit senior citizens in my constituency who receive old age assistance or old age security. I have seen the dire necessity occasioned in most cases by living in larger places where much of the pension or assistance, is consumed by rent. I have seen the need of these people who have borne the heat of the day and instead of spending their lives in a measure of security and comfort exist with a great deal of discomfort lacking in many cases the bare necessities of life. I am sure that all hon. members have received correspondence on this question or have seen resolutions from organizations directly concerned with the welfare of senior citizens.
Unemployment, the needs of veterans and the needs of our senior citizens are problems that face us. Then, we have our civil servants who in many cases are receiving salaries below the prevailing rates in the districts in which they live. The evidence of the need of that increase is to be found by anyone who has read the excellent briefs brought to the attention of the government and hon. members. I am unfamiliar with all of the details as to the schedule of salaries, details as to the classifications, and so forth, but after reading those briefs I am distinctly of the opinion that our civil servants are entitled to adjustments in their salaries, wages and so on. We are glad that the government has at last started to recognize the just claims of the civil servants. Here is another group, a very important group in Canada rendering a service to this country, which has placed before the government its needs with respect to salary adjustments. I mention these few important segments of our population only to illustrate the points I wish to make. There are others, but time will not permit me to deal with them now.


What are the facts in relation to, shall I say, our opportunity to meet this demonstrated need? I do want to make it clear that I am not one who believes in unsound finance. By that I mean I recognize that budgets generally, except in times of emergency, as far as current revenue and current expenditure are concerned, should be balanced, and the suggestions I wish to make will be along these lines. I am not one who has lived on what you would call a bed of comfort all my life. I have known what hard work is, saving my pennies for a rainy day. That sort of experience inclines one to be fairly sound when making suggestions dealing with financial matters.
But what are the facts? I have stated some of the needs that have to be met. This year, as I heard the minister, it is estimated our gross national product will be $54.6 billion. The minister informed us that an amount equal to a quarter of that would be capital invested in Canada this year. The minister also informed us that in 1959 we had the largest exports in the history of Canada. Last year, when we had somewhere between 500,000 and 900,000 unemployed in this country, we exported $5 billion worth of goods, and we want exports. That is the position of the government as a whole with respect to the gross national product, anticipated capital investments in 1960, and the export situation last year which the minister expects to be improved this year.
What about profits? I am going to give only three or four illustrations. Last year was a most profitable year for business people in Canada. Since we live under the capitalist system I am not one to suggest for a moment that it is a criminal offence to make a profit because I realize business cannot exist under capitalism without making a profit. But I do want to bring to the attention of the house the excellent showing that some of the companies made last year, and' the possibility this offers for the Minister of Finance when he is looking for funds to meet the needs that I have mentioned.
The Bell Telephone Company, the largest privately owned company in Canada, showed a net profit of more than $50 million, which was 29.3 per cent over the year 1958. The British Columbia Telephone Company, which we dealt with recently in the form of a bill presented to the house, second in size to the Bell Telephone Company, had a net profit in 1959 of $6.6 million, over 60 per cent higher than in 1958. The New Brunswick Telephone Company, privately owned, showed a net profit of more than $2 million in 1959; this was 33.7 per cent more than in 1958.

Let us take a look at a few of the other large corporations. Dominion Tar and Chemical had a good year, with a net profit of 53.8 per cent over 1958, amounting to $11 million. The British American Oil Company had a net profit in 1959 amounting to over $25 million, a 25 per cent increase over the year 1958. Abitibi Power and Paper Company showed a net profit of $11.8 million for 1959, a 22.5 per cent increase over 1958. International Nickel had a net profit of $85 million in 1959, more than double the 1958 profit.
I suggest that not only is it the duty of the opposition to criticize the government's policy or policies but to offer constructive alternatives to government policy. Before doing that I want to say that I have thought very seriously about this question because over the years I have come to the conclusion that time is running out for those who refuse to recognize the changes that are taking place. On the one hand, we have a growing economic dictatorship known as monopoly capitalism which is daily freezing out the genuinely free enterprise practised by small manufacturers and businessmen. This is occurring in every part of this country. On the other hand, we have the political dictatorship of communism.
We in the C.C.F. group, believing in democratic principles, believing in parliamentary institutions, believe there is a middle course. We call it a dual or mixed economy, representing an understanding of human nature, Canadian psychology, Canadian history and Canadian traditions, and that we can do something to find a middle way between those two extremes before it is too late. This is why this group continues to put forward to the house the policies it does. Unless we do this, Mr. Speaker, there is a day coming- and it is not far off-when there is going to be a clash between extreme views, because if you remove all the economic diversification from democratic society you will have placed democratic society into two clearly defined groups; on the one side the monopolistic owners, and on the other side the workers recognizing the fact that that is the position they must continue to occupy in society for all time.
How can we meet those current needs that I have mentioned? I have made these rough calculations. I am not suggesting that they are exact but I think they are approximately exact. I will deal with current account first. I think that any person who goes into debt for his needs is going to become bankrupt very soon. When it comes to current account we have to pay as we go, and we can do that and provide for the needs of the people of this country.

I estimate that a 33-J- per cent increase in disability pensions will cost $50 million. The amount required under the War Veterans Allowance Act will cost approximately $7 million. To pay our senior citizens at this time-I am suggesting this figure-an extra $10 a month to which they are entitled would cost $130 million. The cost of increasing our civil servants' salaries I am going to place at $50 million. That makes a total of $237 million that we have to find for this current account expense involved in carrying on the day to day life of these people. Can we do it? With revenue estimated by the minister this year of $5,892 million, $237 million does not seem a very large figure to satisfy the needs of these very large groups in our society. We suggest that these needs can be met. They can be met first, as we say in our amendment, by the planned elimination of wasteful defence expenditures, and for a start we will use the figure of $300 million. I believe there is a reduction this year of around $90 million in defence expenditures.
We in this group are quite confident that every dollar that is being spent on the Bomarc is being wasted. We are quite confident that if the government pruned wasteful defence expenditure we could save $300 million for a start, and I think I am very conservative with that estimate. Not only do I say that but I predict that this government will be doing just that inside of a year or two because of the change of circumstances with defence.
We also urge an appropriate provision for a capital gains tax. This is a rather difficult tax to estimate. I have gone to a number of sources for information, and I estimate that we can obtain approximately $100 million a year from that tax. There is such a tax in the United States and the United Kingdom, and for the life of me I cannot see why a person should win $100,000 in a sweepstake and not pay a cent of tax while some poor chap working hard every day has to pay income tax if he earns above a certain level. There is a large field for the operation of a capital gains tax. When we refer to an appropriate capital gains tax we are not suggesting for a moment that we should take away the benefits that a man derives when he sells his home or farm property and moves from one place to another, but there are appropriate areas in which a capital gains tax can be applied.
According to the figures I have drawn up that makes a total of about $400 million as against requirements of $237 million. We in this group are definitely of the opinion that by taking that course we can, without any

The Budget-Mr. Herridge imbalance of the budget, provide for these people who are appealing to the government for assistance and help at this time to remedy their present circumstances.
What about unemployment? I have left unemployment to the last because we in this group are of the opinion that unemployment, continuing problem that it is and related as it is to fiscal, investment and resource development policies, is not going to be solved out of current revenue. It will have to be solved as the result of a national investment program.
What do we need in this young country? There is need for a national highways system. I am not going to deal with that fully because I think there is a bill still before the house. But we have only to read a number of publications and resolutions in recent days to realize the enormous amount of money we are losing in tourist trade because of our highway system in Canada. The main reason for our unfavourable balance at the present time as far as the tourist industry is concerned is the condition of our highways in Canada. That is indicated in United States publications.
We need hospitals. My goodness, in the city of Ottawa people cannot get into a hospital. I have heard of people waiting for 10 days, two weeks and so on, and that condition prevails in many places. Should that condition prevail in a civilized society producing the immense amount of wealth that we are? We also need schools. There is a great need for rural redevelopment, which this government has recognized. At this point I want to say that I have been very interested in reading the proceedings of the Senate committee dealing with land use in Canada. 1 think they are doing very useful work. That is the sort of thing that can be done very well by the Senate. They can take their time, and I am not saying that in a jocular sense. Studies of this sort are not easily made by members of the house when they are burdened with the work of the house committees and correspondence. I think the members of the Senate committee are doing very useful work and as a result have obtained some most useful information.
There is a tremendous need in Canada for rural redevelopment and for the relocation of about 25 per cent of the farming population from marginal to satisfactory economic farm units. This has been proceeding in the United States. This is a field in which something practical can be done as a result of federal, provincial and community co-operation.
Look at the need for power. Look at the difficulty we are having in British Columbia


and with respect to the development of that great natural resource, the Columbia river. Look at the opportunity there for the federal and provincial governments.
It is for that reason that we propose the provision of a self-liquidating public investment program. As long as it is self-liquidating it is a sound program because it is for the development and utilization of natural resources which brings returns. In doing so we bring together to the advantage of the community as a whole idle human resources and idle natural resources.
It will require planned fiscal and development policies to overcome the unemployment that is with us at this time and which will continue with us in any circumstances under our present system. We in this group say this. Because we believe in this mixed economy we believe that governments, whether federal or provincial, have to face the fact that they have to take the leadership with respect to the public sector of the economy. There is a public sector that definitely requires development. We say, let the private banks supply the capital needs and the capital requirements of the private sector of industry and development in this country and let the Bank of Canada supply the credit that is required for a national investment program.
The security is there as has been evidenced in recent years. Mr. Wenner-Gren comes to British Columbia and gets an option, as it were, on 40,000 square miles of British Columbia with huge water resources, huge forest resources, huge land resources, in short, an empire. What did his representatives do when they came before the Senate committee last year? For what did they plead? Mr. Main-waring's adopted children came before the Senate committee and wanted the government to impose export of power taxation by order in council so they could bargain with any government in the future as to the taxes they would pay. They came before this committee and definitely said they were going to raise $500 million. What is the security? The natural resources of the people of British Columbia.
It is the same with the pulp and paper industry. One company in that province gets a timber management licence and is immediately able to go to New York and raise $200 million. What is the security? The natural resources owned by the people. We have hydro companies doing the same thing. We say that people seem to be hypnotized by the idea that money can only be created by private institutions. Under these circumstances the lending of money is a racket and an imposition on the people of this

country. I am not blaming the individuals concerned. The responsibility does not rest on them. Things are changed when enough people understand the situation and are alerted to it.
What we say is this. Why not use the national credit of Canada through the Bank of Canada, using the natural resources of Canada as the security or the base for a national investment and development program? We suggest that is one way in which to provide stability and more regularity of income in this country. It can be planned between the federal government and the provinces to All up the gaps in unemployment at the most serious periods.
This afternoon, when the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) was speaking he mentioned our responsibility to the underdeveloped nations and the fact that democracy was challenged throughout the world. That is another aspect of our program that we believe in. The hon. member mentioned the disparity of annual income, between an average of $2,000 a year on the North American continent and $60 a year in India. There is no question about it, that situation cannot continue indefinitely. In the ordinary process of economics it will destroy us through an expanding population.
Democratic institutions are in danger. If we are going to meet our responsibilities abroad and do the things at home that are required at this time and in the future full production is essential to meet the needs.
I am nearing the end of my speech, Mr. Speaker, I have not had the opportunity to go into detail but I suggest that these are some of the alternative proposals, put forward by this party in order to provide full production in Canada and consequently full employment and to provide an opportunity for the government to fulfil its obligations to Canadians at home and needy persons abroad.
In conclusion, may I say this? We ask the government and the minister to give serious consideration to these proposals advanced in good faith.

Mr. Speaker, my first
words must be directed to paying respects to you on behalf of my electors and myself, having regard to the honoured position you hold in this house. I also at this time want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) on the excellent budget he brought down one week ago tonight. I think this budget is appropriate and sane. We have heard a great deal of criticism, one way or another; but when we look back over the last three years we find that we inherited a recession which, had it not been for the
The Budget-Mr. Barrington good work of the present government under the capable leadership of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), could easily have developed into a depression and a severe one at that.

I think a further proof of the value of this budget as it has been brought down and of how well it has been received by the electorate in general across Canada is shown by the criticism made by the opposition. The criticism of the opposition that I have heard to date-and I think I am a fairly regular attendant here in the house-reminds me somewhat of the housewife who is trying to make gravy without grease. It is not all going to happen at once. They understand this fact. They are willing to accept it. I have the honour to represent three counties in the province of Quebec, namely the counties of Chateauguay, Huntingdon and Laprairie. This being my maiden speech in the house I should like to take hon. members on a short tour through my constituency.
The counties are located in the southwestern part of Quebec and are bordered by

The Budget-Mr. Barrington the St. Lawrence seaway on the east and by the county of Beauharnois-Salaberry on the north, the remainder being bordered by the state of New York and a section of the constituency of St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville.
As the county of Laprairie has a population composed to the extent of some 90 per cent of French speaking Canadians, I am pleased to represent my electorate there in the French language.

Laprairie constituency is located on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, directly opposite the city of Montreal. As will therefore easily be realized, it represents an important section of the St. Lawrence seaway. Cote Ste. Catherine, the Laprairie basin, Candiac, Caughnawaga-are all places that we often hear about and which are situated in this important constituency. Farms and beaches along the river have all vanished from that area, as did the beautiful scenery of the great St. Lawrence. Many sites have been bought for future industrial expansion; a large industrial centre is under construction there. Population is rapidly increasing and, in this regard, I urge the Postmaster General (Mr. Hamilton) to consider the advisability of providing the electors of Laprairie with a letter carrier service.
Already, with the St. Lawrence seaway, the numerous railways, the well kept roads, the riding has become an ideal site for the development of new industries, and I intend to do all I can to attract new industries and, at the same time, to co-operate fully with the authorities in this regard.
I have in mind something you have probably heard about, and I refer to a project as important as the St. Lawrence seaway itself. You have probably guessed that I mean the deepening of the Richelieu river. The Richelieu will be deepened some day. It has to be done because the whole country needs it, because we need it and our neighbours to the south need it too. Some people suggest deepening the Richelieu from Sorel as far as lake Champlain. Others believe it would be more advantageous and more useful to dredge this canal inland, from Ste. Therese island on the Richelieu to the vicinity of Longueuil.
I have a third project in mind. I refer to a canal starting at Ste. Therese island, on the Richelieu, and cutting through the land to the area just outside Laprairie. One of the great benefits from such a scheme would be to shorten the distances and reduce construction costs. Moreover, the canal would end up in a


new area, where it would be easy to do some city planning and provide appropriate residential, commercial and industrial zoning. This third project would obviously be of considerable benefit not only to the city of Laprairie but also to the surrounding area, on the south shore, and to the whole constituency.

Mr. Speaker, my home county is the county of Chateauguay, the county where history was made on October 26, 1813 when Colonel Charles-Michel de Salaberry, with a few hundred soldiers and a friendly band of Indians, won immortal fame by successfully defeating the American invaders who had invaded Lower Canada and were marching on the city of Montreal. This is where the all important battle of Chateauguay was fought and won, and it is one of the great historical sites of our country.
The other county I have the honour to represent is the county of Huntingdon, which stretches from the Indian reserve at St. Regis across the river from Cornwall to the Richelieu river, and has some 50 miles of frontier with our neighbours to the south in the state of New York.
The two counties of Chateauguay-Hunting-don form what is known as the Chateauguay valley, and here dairy farming is the principal industry. In fact, it is considered to be one of the more important of its kind in the whole of Canada. Here a large percentage of the fluid milk consumed in the city of Montreal is produced. We have excellent soil and growing conditions, and all in all it is considered a very prosperous farming community.
Great pride is taken in the fine dairy herds raised throughout this area, and we have a good export market to the United States of purebred cattle and other livestock. In fact, it is not uncommon for cattle to be shipped from this area to such places as South America and many of the other Latin countries.
If I may be permitted to insert a little commercialism at this time I should like to say that in this fertile and prosperous valley, to be more explicit, my home town of Ormstown, Quebec, each year is held an agricultural and livestock exhibition. It is held in the second week in June and I would like to take this opportunity, through you, sir, to invite anyone interested in a good livestock and agricultural exhibition to be my guest at this fair, which is often called the Little Royal, and is known as the biggest fair in the smallest town in Canada.

As I have stated, the main industry in the counties I have the honour to represent is that of dairy farming. Dairy farming is a subject we hear very little about in this house. I have been rather disappointed, I might say, about this, since I have come into the house. We hear a great deal of another type of farming, but I fear we do not hear enough about the dairy farming industry.
I should like at this time to discuss this industry, but first let us take a look at the man who operates as a dairy farmer. What is he made up of? What kind of individual is he? There are two words which answer this question: he is a hard-working man. A dairy farmer today starts before sunrise and goes long after sunset. To be a successful dairy farmer a man must not only be hardworking but must be practically a jack of all trades and master of many. For example, he must be, in part, a veterinarian, an agronomist, a machinist. He has to be an expert in so many fields and in a goodly number of them he must be highly qualified.
We hear statements that the dairy farmer is enjoying great prosperity. With this I cannot agree. He has possibly shown a certain degree of prosperity in the last few years. But this has all come about by good management and efficiency on his part. The way things are in the dairy farming industry today, the dairy farmer is not getting the protection that other industries are enjoying. We know we have surpluses in dairy farm products, but I think these surpluses are because of the efficiency of the dairy farmer. We know that in the last few years he has been able to produce more; he has been able to place his commodity on the market, and I think especially of butter where a surplus has been built up of this product. Very well. Suppose this surplus has been built up due to the efficiency of the farmer. Why should the farmer be penalized because he is an efficient operator? We have to find a cure for this situation.
The dairy farmer has a great deal with which to contend. He must face many difficulties. He has to gamble with the weather. He has to gamble with the moods of the people in general, and he has a difficult market in which to compete. Workers in other spheres-workers in industry, for example-can go on strike through their labour unions if they are not happy about the way things are going. But the farmer would look very foolish if he decided to go on strike, closed down the valves on his cows and sent them out on the picket line. It would be a pretty foolish operation.

He is at the mercy of the public. He cannot obtain protection in the same way as other workers are protected, although the whole rural economy, especially in the eastern part of Canada depends on the dairy farmer. I think it is so true, the saying we often hear, that as the dairy farmer goes, so goes the nation. If the dairy farmer is enjoying prosperity, the whole district around him is sharing that prosperity. The dairy farmer is, no doubt, the backbone of our country. Maybe this country is gradually becoming more industrialized, but anyone who believes that a day will come when there will be no such thing as a dairy farmer had better give the matter further thought. The dairy farmer is the backbone of the country and I am certain he will continue to be so for many years to come.
With regard to this question of surpluses, I should like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) and to the government as a whole. As I have just said, I do not feel that the efficiency of the dairy farmer should be a reason for penalizing him in the end. I ask the Minister of Agriculture, whose dairy farm policy will, we know, be brought into the house in the very near future, to hold the line, especially with regard to the price of butter. I ask him to take no action as a result of which the dairy farmer will suffer. Let the minister retain the present measure of support. Everyone knows we cannot go on forever buying up surpluses. No government can do that. But I should like to suggest that the government appoint a commission to work with the dairy farmers of Canada through their group leaders to study this question in the coming year to try to arrange matters so that a balance between supply and demand with regard to this product can be attained. Butter is very important to the economy of the eastern dairy farm, and the future of the whole dairy industry depends on this product.
Now I should like to say a few words about another industry which I have in my constituency, namely the textile industry which plays an important part in the lives of my constituents both in Chateauguay and Huntingdon counties, especially in the towns of Huntingdon and Ormstown. As in other such localities, we are very much concerned about the future of this vital industry. We know that since the Progressive Conservative party has been in power a great improvement has been noted. We realize that there is still more to be done.
The former government criticized the textile industry, saying it was inefficient and poorly managed. It was ready to abandon

The Budget-Mr. Barrington ship and let the industry sink. We know that the present government has no such intention. I am happy to say that the textile industry in the two towns I have mentioned, Huntingdon and Ormstown, is under the best of management, well organized and efficient. Sometimes when we speak of the textile industry I think we forget the very important part it plays in the life of our country.
We find that the primary textile industry, especially in the province of Quebec, is located in the smaller municipalities. When there is a shutdown at the mill, there is a shutdown in the town. This affects the merchant, the butcher, and the grocer; the whole financial set-up in the town is disturbed. When we consider that some of these smaller plants are established in towns with populations of 2,000, 2,200, or 2,800 people, one can imagine the effect upon all concerned when the mills are shut down. We cannot allow that to happen.
I know the Minister of Finance has given a great deal of thought to this problem and that he is still working hard on it. I have heard directly from the management of the mills I have mentioned that they are very pleased with the action the minister has taken to date. They know he is sincere and that he intends to do his level best to improve the situation, but I ask the minister this: even if it is necessary to take what might be considered in some quarters to be drastic action, he should take such action for the benefit of this all-important industry. As I have stated, many of the smaller municipalities are directly affected. Again, on behalf of the employers and employees engaged in the textile industries in my area, I ask the government to take very definite steps to improve the situation.
In the same breath, I want to thank the government on behalf of the employers and employees in this industry for the steps which have been taken in the past month to come to its aid. I sincerely hope that this assistance will continue until such time as this industry will enjoy the prosperity it once knew and deserves. As my final words on this subject, I would say if this industry is to survive in the smaller municipalities and small towns the assistance and aid must come now.
I bring these matters to the attention of hon. members, first, in order to represent my electors who have placed their confidence and trust in me by electing me as a member of this house and, second, in order that it be known that the counties of Chateauguay-Huntingdon-Laprairie do in fact exist. I regret to say this, but facts are facts and let us put the cards on the table. In past years my counties were poorly represented by the

elected member who in the apparent custom of the day sat on the laurels of a sympathetic vote and forgot the needs of the electors. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, this is not the pattern I shall follow either in this house or in representing my electors outside this house.

Mr. Speaker, like my colleagues, I should like to make a few remarks to express the feeling of the taxpayers I represent here. In the constituency of Drummond-Arthabaska, as in many others, there are two sectors of economic activity which determine the prosperity of its inhabitants: the textile and farming industries.
The matter on which I should like to call the attention of the house, and most particularly that of the Minister of Finance, is that of the textile industry.
The question has given rise to many newspaper comments, especially lately. It shows the importance of the textile industry in Canada, and particularly in eastern Quebec and in Ontario.
That industry, one of Canada's major industries, has been an essential factor in Canada's economic development.
According to figures published in the statistical year book, 1959 edition, in 1956 we had 3,786 establishments engaged in the textile industry, including 965 in primary manufacturing processes, 296 in knitting, and 2,525 in garment making.
Those 3,786 establishments employed 182,575 people, and produced close to $1,700 million worth of goods. It is hard to get statistical data for 1959, to compare with the figures I have just quoted.

In spite of the best efforts of our industrialists and workers who wish to maintain their industries in operation, several of them gave up or moved to other countries. I respect that point of view, but the hard fact remains that there are close to 200,000 employees in our textile industries. If we deprive them of their means of subsistence, Canada's economy will be jeopardized, and western farmers may be the first to suffer.
We must also think of the 93,000 young people who enter the labour market every year. What can we offer them as compensation for the jobs we would be exporting through increases in our purchases abroad?
After all, we should not have to buy them a ticket to Japan or Hong Kong.
Mr. Speaker, to assess the possible effects on our economy of the government's failure to protect our secondary and primary industries-and I am thinking of textiles-we need only look at a study made by Canadian National economists in the city of Stratford, Ontario, on the economic impact to be expected from the creation of new jobs for 100 workers. It is shown that those 100 new jobs would provide a living for 131 families or 427 individuals.
Those 100 jobs would create 117 other nonindustrial jobs, and finally, would raise the annual purchasing power at retail prices by $939,000.
There is no doubt that if the investigation had been continued into the possible effects of the creation of 200 new jobs, the resulting figures would have been more than doubled.
Mr. Speaker, it cannot be denied that the situation of the textile industry is alarming in Canada. It is alarming for two reasons: excessive imports and ineffective anti-dumping legislation.
What future is there for our textile industries? That will depend on the share of the Canadian market that is reserved for our domestic industry in relation to imports.
